# Rubea autem metalla in colore admixtione diuersa sunt a dictis: sicut satis ostendimus cum de coloribus metallorum ageret. 

Habet autem ferrum secundum se specialem determinationem extra alia elementa. Dicamus igitur eris compositionem supponentes que iam dudum probata sunt omne metallum ex sulphure componi & argento viuo. Ponamus igitur argentum viuum esse bonum non feculentum siue lutulentum, no[n] tamen ab humore extraneo omnino purgatum: substantiam sulphuris esse feculentam & adurentem & in parte accensam: sicut argento viuo per substantiam & qualitates commisceri. nunc enim absque dubio conuertit ipsum in ruborem & non poterit eidem propter utriusque non plenam subtiliationem bene misceri / tunc efficiet es quod non est omnino bone mixtionis. propter quod multa fer inde resoluitur / & multum euaporat in igne quia cum sulphur in parte incensum est. ideo quedam partes argenti viui amplius quam alie purificatur & consumit in eis superfluum humidum & in illis partibus videbitur habere venas auri. In alijs autem ubi minus digestum est erit scalosum & ignobile & terrestre propter adustionem / & hanc diuersitatem in cupro quod inuenitur in theutonicis partibus in loco qui <margin>Goslaria</margin> goslaria vocatur expresse inuenimus. & ideo etiam hoc cuprum melius omnibus alijs estimatur tanquam venas auri habens immixtas / & non est improbabile quin sulphur illi eris sit mictu cum arsenico rubeo in aliqua quantitate. & ideo sit magis adurens sulphur illius metalli quam alterius.

<margin>Cupru[m] i[n] auricalcu[m] vertit[ur]</margin>
Nunc igitur scimus materiam eris / quoniam est metallum ex argento viuo plusquam oportet aliquantulum habens per commixtionem adurentis sulphuris ad formam ruboris deducti / ex qua autem natura sulphur sit adurens in precedentibus satis determinatum est. Arsenicum autem calcinatum sit quidem nigrum ex rubeo / sed postea & sublimatum in alutel quod est vas opertum cum collo alto vt sepius diximus reuertitur album ad instar niuis / & si sepius iterentur talis calcinatio & sublimatio tunc efficitur multum album & acutissimum / & ex acumine eri coniunctum liquando penetrat in ipsum & conuertit in candorem. si tamen diu stet in igne es expirabit arsenicum & tunc redit pristinus color cupri sicut de facili probatur in alchimicis. Hi autem qui in cupro multum operantur in nostris partibus parisius videlicet & colonie & in alijs locis in quibus fui & vidi experiri uertunt cuprum in auricalcum per puluerem lapidis qui calamina vocatur. & cum euaporat lapis adhuc remanet splendor obscurus declinans aliquantulum ad auri speciem. Vt autem albius efficiatur & ita citrinitati auri magis sit simile immiscet aliquantulum de stagno. propter que etiam auricalcum multum de ductibilitate cupri amittit. Et illi qui decipere volunt & splendorem similem auro inducere ligant lapidem: ita quod diutius remanet in ere in igne no[n] euaporans cito ab ere. 

Ligatur autem per oleum vitri tostatur enim fragmenta vitri & conuertuntur in puluerem & spargitur in testam super es postquam immissa est calamina / & tunc vitrum piectum enatat super es & non sinit euaporare lapidem & lapidis virtutem: sed reflectit vaporem lapidis in es. & sic dumque fortiter purgat es & adurunt in eo materie feculente. Tandem tamen euaporat etiam oleum vitri. & tunc euaporat virtus lapidis / sed auricalcum efficitur multo splendidius quam esset sine illo. Qui aut[em] adhuc amplius assimilare auro intendit. has purgationes per opesum & vitri oleum sepius iterat / & loco Auricalci stagni ponit argentum & immiscet auricalco. Et hoc efficit ita rutilum cum colore citrinum quod multi credunt ipsum esse aurum cum in veritate adhuc remaneat sit in specie eris. 

<margin>Hermes</margin>
Hermes autem dicit quod si eri liquefacto tuchia puluerizata siue sit tuchia alba siue rubea quod ipsum in colorem auri conuertit. Quid autem sit tuchia in sequenti libro ubi de medijs aget dicetur. sed hic sufficiat est quod tuchie adustione assumitur terrestreitas & purgat ab ere superfluum humidum ipsius. & ideo tunc erit pulchrius. tamen & virtus tuchie euaporat per ignem si diu steterit in igne. & ideo nisi aliud medicamen fuerit euaporabit tuchia. & tunc erit pristinus color cupri. Dicit etiam Hermes cum quo concordant experta. quod si es tale aspersum super acetum vel vrinam pueri masculi virginis locet penetrabit virtus urine siue aceti substantiam eris & conuertet ipsum in virorem. Si autem iterum per se solum es locetur super racemos expressos solo vapore vini conuertetur in optimum colorem viridem plucentez. Si autem huic colori auripigmentum siue arsenicum approximatur & precipue adustum condemnando destruit virorem & inducit colorem fuscum terrestrem ad opacitatem declinantem. Huius causa autem ex dictis facile manifestatur. est enim sal aperitiuum / & ideo aperit cupri substantiam seque si in tenues laminas deductum sit / & tunc vapor acetus aceti vel urine incendit ipsum: quod tamen est a sulphure nimis accenso. propter quod humidum terrestre adiunctum leue quod est ignitum in ipso virore accipit sicut colera calidissima & pessima que est sicut erugo eris vt dicunt medici. Quoniam autem primo vapor non est adeo acutus sicut vapor vini coniuncti / tunc non ita intensam inducit rubedinem. & ideo manet auri color placidus. Auripigmentum autem est excellen[ter] adurens & ideo cum hoc approximat substantie sic colorate comburet modicum humidum quod est in ipso. & tunc manet quod est terrestre opacum. per eundem modum quo etiam colera adusta relinquit cinerem melancolicum accidentalem calidissime melancolie secundum experta medicine. Tanta igitur de eris natura & effectibus dicta sunt.

### Capitulum octauum de natura & admixtione auri.

<meta>The previous page concluded the discussion on the nature of silver, focusing on its purity and its relationship to quicksilver. This page transitions into the "red metals," specifically iron and copper, explaining their composition and the alchemical processes used to alter their appearance to resemble gold or produce pigments like verdigris.</meta>

<sig>n ij</sig>

# Red metals, however, are different in their color and mixture from those already mentioned: as we have sufficiently shown when we dealt with the colors of metals.

Iron has a specific nature of its own beyond the other elements. Let us therefore speak of the composition of **copper** <note>original: "eris"; here referring to copper or its alloys</note>, assuming what has long been proven: that every metal is composed of **sulfur** and **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>. Let us suppose that the quicksilver is good and not dreggy or muddy, yet not entirely purged of external moisture. Let the substance of the sulfur be dreggy, burning, and partially ignited, just as it is mixed with the quicksilver in substance and quality. For now, without doubt, it turns the quicksilver red; because both are not fully refined, they cannot mix well. Then it creates copper, which is not of an entirely good mixture. Because of this, much of it is consumed and much evaporates in the fire, since the sulfur is partially burnt. Therefore, some parts of the quicksilver are purified more than others, and the superfluous moisture in them is consumed; in those parts, it will seem to have **veins of gold**. In other parts, however, where it is less "digested" <term>digestio; the natural "cooking" or ripening of minerals in the earth</term>, it will be scaly, base, and earthy due to the burning. We have clearly found this diversity in the copper found in the German regions, in the place called <margin>Goslar</margin> **Goslar**. Therefore, this copper is esteemed better than all others, as if having veins of gold mixed in. It is not improbable that the sulfur of that copper is mixed with red **arsenic** in some quantity, and therefore the sulfur of that metal is more "burning" than that of others.

<margin>Copper is turned into brass</margin>
Now we know the material of copper: it is a metal made from quicksilver, having a bit more than is proper through the mixture of burning sulfur, which leads it to a red form. The nature by which sulfur is "burning" has been sufficiently determined in what preceded. **Arsenic**, when calcined <note>heated to a high temperature to remove volatile substances</note>, turns black from red; but afterward, when **sublimated** <note>turned into vapor and then solidified</note> in an **alutel** <note>original: "alutel"; a pear-shaped vessel used in alchemy for sublimation</note>, which is a covered vessel with a high neck as we have often said, it returns white like snow. If such calcination and sublimation are repeated often, it becomes very white and very sharp. Because of this sharpness, when joined to copper by melting, it penetrates it and turns it white. However, if it stays in the fire a long time, the copper will "breathe out" the arsenic, and then the original color of the copper returns, as is easily proven in alchemical works. Those who work much with copper in our regions—namely in Paris, Cologne, and other places where I have been and seen experiments—turn copper into **brass** <note>original: "auricalcum"; orichalcum</note> by using the powder of a stone called **calamine** <note>zinc ore</note>. When the stone evaporates, a dim splendor still remains, inclining somewhat toward the appearance of gold. To make it whiter and thus more similar to the yellow of gold, they mix in a little **tin**. Because of this, the brass loses much of the ductility <note>the ability to be hammered thin or drawn into wire</note> of the copper. Those who wish to deceive and induce a splendor similar to gold "bind" the stone so that it remains longer in the copper in the fire and does not evaporate quickly.

It is "bound" by **glass oil**: fragments of glass are toasted and turned into powder, which is sprinkled into the crucible over the copper after the calamine has been put in. Then the melted glass floats over the copper and does not allow the stone or its virtue to evaporate; instead, it reflects the vapor of the stone back into the copper. Thus, for a while, it strongly purges the copper and burns away the dreggy materials in it. Eventually, however, even the glass oil evaporates, and then the virtue of the stone evaporates; but the brass is made much more splendid than it would be without it. He who intends to make it resemble gold even more repeats these purgings with the glass oil often, and in place of tin, he takes **silver** and mixes it with the brass. This makes it so ruddy and yellow in color that many believe it to be gold, though in truth it remains in the species of copper.

<margin>Hermes</margin>
**Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> says that if powdered **tutty** <note>original: "tuchia"; zinc oxide collected from smelting furnaces</note>, whether white or red, is added to melted copper, it converts it to the color of gold. What tutty is will be discussed in the following book where we deal with intermediate substances. But let it suffice here that by the "burning" of the tutty, the earthiness is removed and it purges the copper of its superfluous moisture; therefore, it will then be more beautiful. However, the virtue of the tutty also evaporates through fire if it stands in the fire for a long time. Unless another "medicine" <note>an additive or reagent</note> is used, the tutty will evaporate, and then the original color of the copper returns. Hermes also says, and experience agrees, that if such copper is sprinkled with vinegar or the urine of a virgin male child, the virtue of the urine or vinegar will penetrate the substance of the copper and turn it green. If, however, the copper is placed by itself over pressed grape skins, it will be converted into an excellent, shining green color by the vapor of the wine alone. But if **orpiment** <note>original: "auripigmentum"; a yellow arsenic ore</note> or arsenic is brought near this color, especially if it is burnt, it destroys the green and induces a dark, earthy color inclining toward opacity. The cause of this is easily shown from what has been said. For salt is opening, and therefore it opens the substance of the copper, especially if it has been hammered into thin plates; then the sharp vapor of the vinegar or urine ignites it, which comes from the overly-ignited sulfur. Because of this, the light earthy moisture joined to it, which is ignited, takes on that greenness, much like the hottest and worst bile which physicians call the "rust of copper." Since at first the vapor is not as sharp as the vapor of joined wine, it does not induce such an intense redness, and so the gold color remains pleasant. Orpiment, however, is excellently "burning," and so when it approaches a substance colored this way, it burns the small amount of moisture in it; then what remains is the earthy opacity. This is the same way that burnt bile leaves behind a "melancholic ash," according to medical experience. Thus, so much has been said concerning the nature and effects of copper.

### Chapter Eight: On the nature and admixture of gold.

<summary>This page explains the chemical nature of copper as a mix of sulfur and mercury, detailing how medieval craftsmen in cities like Paris and Cologne used calamine, arsenic, and tutty to create brass or gold-like imitations. It also describes the production of verdigris (green pigment) through the reaction of copper with acidic vapors like vinegar or wine.</summary>

# Book Six

<margin>The sea and the hidden rivers</margin>
the sea receives an entrance, as it holds just as much space there; or perhaps even more, since the upper regions had to be shared with so many living creatures. Desolate places, even without an inhabitant, float more freely on the waves. Who would prevent the waters from fluctuating there and being driven by the winds, which every interval of the earth and every space of air creates? Therefore, a storm, having arisen greater than usual, can shake a part of the earth, having been driven more vehemently. For among us, too, many places that had been far from the sea were suddenly struck by its approach, and the waves invaded villas placed within view, which were heard from afar. There, too, the sea can retreat and uncover the lower depths, which does not happen without a movement of the substance. I do not believe you will hesitate for long to believe that there are subterranean rivers and a hidden sea. For whence do these things spring? Whence do they come to us, if not because the origin of moisture is contained within? Come, when you see the <term>Tigris</term> <gloss>a great river in Western Asia</gloss> interrupted, drying up in the middle of its course—and it is not turned away entirely, but diminishes little by little as the waters become invisible, and then is consumed—where do you think it goes, if not into the dark places of the earth? Especially since you see it emerge again, no smaller than the one that had flowed before. What of when you see the <term>Alpheus</term> <gloss>a river in Greece</gloss>, celebrated by the poets in Achaia, submerged, and then pouring forth in Sicily, after having crossed the sea, the most pleasant fountain of <term>Arethusa</term> <gloss>a nymph transformed into a fountain</gloss>? Moreover, you are not unaware that among the opinions held by those who narrate the flooding of the <term>Nilus</term> <gloss>the Nile river</gloss>, one is that it breaks forth and increases from the earth, not from waters above, but from those returned from the depths. Indeed, I myself <note>referring to the historian's own experience or report</note> have seen two centurions whom Nero Caesar, a man who loves truth as much as he loves other virtues, had sent to investigate the source of the Nile.

<summary>Seneca discusses subterranean waters, the connectivity of hidden seas, and the mysterious sources of rivers like the Tigris and the Nile.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological and grammatical analysis from the previous section. While the earlier text focused on how nouns relate to objects of desire or specific animals, this page delves deeper into the technical mechanics of the Greek language—specifically pronouns, the morphology of verbs of motion, and the etymological roots of psychological states like madness and melancholy. The presence of Vatican stamps suggests this manuscript was a part of a scholarly collection, likely used by a Byzantine commentator to explain the dense philosophical vocabulary of Marcus Aurelius or a similar Stoic text.</meta>

# Meditations
## On Grammar, Motion, and the Afflictions of the Mind

**Column 1**

There is a deception even regarding the name **apolic** <note>original: *apollikēn*; the term is obscure, possibly referring to a name that is "removed" or "distant" from its object</note>. What belongs to one, it says, but much is that which is equal to being. Among equals. A name was given to things that exist. The form is derived from these. This is what we say. A pretext <unclear>s'</unclear> of blame, for these are not those things by which they measure, from which we name things in some way. But those things of private victories. To seek a name in this way. In which also to remain. This was better said of common things. But the external, is it possible? The "splendid" used <term>catachrestically</term> <note>original: *katachrēstikōs*, the use of a word in a sense different from its proper one, like calling a "silver" cup "golden"</note> of common things. For the one who shares frequently tends to follow it.

And immediately after this: speak concerning **structure**; as many things as he sees regarding structure in a single way. And there is a humble thing of his, the steps. It is itself, and one will find it. It is equal. What kind of thing is the <term>pronoun</term> <note>original: *antōnymia*</note>, and its feminine form, "this woman." And "that man" and "that woman" for example. For it is not first for him. It is used <term>infinitively</term> <note>original: *aparemphatikōs*</note>. For the whole of... the whole, but no <term>pronoun</term> happens [to match]. It is <term>deictic</term> <note>original: *deiktikon*, pointing or demonstrative</note>. Or if it does not show more, "these things."

For example, "these men," or "these women," or "these men." And the <term>figure</term> <note>original: *schēma*</note> is to proceed. Rich. They do not differ poetically from the formation. Of these, on the one hand, whether it is still something or non-being. Those things, on the other hand, are brief. For example, or if they act. They make it clear. For even the Athenian things—the way of forming them—never once existed. For example: "this man," "herself," but the things regarding the same form do not belong to... for example, to these. And because "this man" is only...

...is. In <term>voice</term> <note>original: *phōnē*</note> it is the thing being said. And it is of the... and this... but all the **doubtful** <note>original: *aporētika*, things causing difficulty or questioning</note> things, they take the "or" in some way. If by **voice** the thing appeared. For it is [necessary] to see how they are. Which one? Adding... to swim. A **thought** <note>original: *noēma*</note> regarding the action here of the two, just as with animals. From which also... themselves are said more than a ship. But the sewing/seam... perhaps, not to go down to those who hear. That man. And that man already goes not, so that that woman would not...

<column-break/>

...other tender tracks. From the word "at the same time." What is this except [this]? So that the beautiful ones <gloss>themselves</gloss> do not always go around. They purify indeed. They always go around. They let go. They release. And they send forth. From the word for "I go" <note>original: *eimi*</note>, the third of the... they go. Whence they... they go. They enter <note>original: *isiasin*</note>, instead of "they go in."

They go out, they fly, they fly, they go down, they go up, they go through, they go towards, they go around, they go away. The "being about to" [future], the "all"... things of "hoping." The "to dwell," and "to remain," after... the "to stretch" <gloss>is transformed</gloss>. Let it not be thought of. Since even "to be afraid" are several things. And yet, you always hope to be; or simply, thus also themselves are of the...

...himself. Not by chance is he such. And it is the same of the **verbs** <note>original: *rhēmatōn*</note>; he heard, "you have ceased"; and the same to whom. So that you said: you fight. From where let us see also from <term>verbs</term> <note>original: *rhēmatōn*</note>. This creation: toward some honor for us through... from which the "made thing" is likely the **wandering**, or **deception**. Instead of "he will go," or "in a trick." A <term>well</term> <note>original: *phreas*</note>. Regarding being springs. Or a well. Just like a well. Where [one is] not in some well. And a well. The thing that flows. Those through a bitter...

...on the one hand, **madness** <note>original: *aponoia*, literally a loss of sense or desperation</note>. "Feed the leaves." The ancient... having placed... water, and every... and... they are the **instruments of the voice**. From which also the sounds of the <term>voice</term> <note>original: *phōnēs*</note> [arise]. Just as for one who speaks much with words, it is **madness** <note>original: *mania*</note>; but the many limbs [of a sentence]. **Melancholy** <note>original: *melancholia*</note>. Of the ancient word, **madness** <note>original: *mania*</note> is common. Or grief. A poetic thing. And the [act of] madness... terrible. The thing that spoke. Or having leaped away. Madness and murder... to be; and from this: his speaking having...

<summary>This page analyzes Greek grammar (pronouns and verbs of motion) and etymology, linking linguistic structure to mental states like madness and melancholy. It uses technical linguistic terms to explain how deception and truth are encoded in speech.</summary>

And if it is large, its edges do not meet because it is circular, spaced apart, and of varying shape, and a lot of meat has been lost from it, so its treatment is suturing and preventing the accumulation of moisture in it by using astringent diluents, and using the plasters that we will mention. If it is deep, then scarring may also stick it together [through] frequent pulling toward the covering. Sometimes the covering gathers... that is where pulling it with a bandage to secure it does not help, as we will show, especially where the firm pulling does not fall on the base of the depth, so materials flow into it because of its weakness. The placement is necessary, and its circumstances are mentioned in the chapter on ulcers. If pulling is needed from its place, place cotton or what serves its function on its face to dry it, especially where the pulling does not fall on the base, [as this is] sufficient for it. And its pouring... its pouring, it is not possible for the bad material to pour off it, or it contains bone or a fracture... and a very bad moisture has arisen from it, and it is then in the category of ulcers rather than abscesses. The scholar said: When the wound needs a bandage that brings the lips together if adhesion and healing are desired. But if it needs meat to grow in it, it does not need that, but it needs, at one time, a bandage that strikes the place, and at another time, a bandage for [the area] behind it, so it does not hold the medicine on it. He said: It is necessary that the position of the wound be a place from which the [superfluity] pours out always by its nature, either by placing the abdomen there, or by shaping it in that shape. For I have seen a large wound, its depth was where I write it, and placing it in the thigh, there it was [the] <term>‘afw</term> <gloss>the healing process</gloss>
and the <term>‘afwah</term> <gloss>the healing process</gloss>

<meta>This page transitions from the general theory of gravity and water seeking its "site of rest" to a specific technical study of fluid dynamics. Here, Leonardo investigates the principle of continuity—the idea that for a vessel to maintain a constant level, the amount of water entering must exactly match the amount exiting.</meta>

<note>First diagram: A horizontal reservoir labeled 'A' feeds water into a vertical cylindrical vessel labeled 'm'. The water then exits from an orifice at the base of 'm'. This setup allows Leonardo to observe how flow rates balance between connected containers.</note>

A pours a <term>mouth</term> <note>original: "bocha"; used here to describe an orifice or the opening of a pipe.</note> of water into m. m pours [from] A,
and it fills with as much <note>Leonardo uses a symbol consisting of a circle with a cross to indicate a proportional relationship or equality.</note> water as exits [at] f
through the opening m; so that it fills m for as much time as
is needed for the water to discharge from its reduced <term>filling</term> <note>original: "rĩpitura"; referring to the volume of liquid contained within the vessel.</note>
[at] m, so that the water in m pours out the water at f.

<margin>
And it will be
understood by way of
m, m, m.
</margin>

<note>Bottom diagrams: Two vertical vessels of different diameters, both labeled 'm'. Leonardo is likely comparing how the width of a container affects the pressure and the time it takes for water to discharge through an outlet of a fixed size.</note>

<summary>A scientific study on the mechanics of water flow between connected vessels. Leonardo concludes that a vessel's water level remains constant when the rate of influx from a source equals the rate of discharge through its outlet.</summary>
<keywords>hydraulics, flow rate, fluid dynamics, vessel volume, orifice, conservation of mass</keywords>

ἀγαθὸς τινὸς πράγματος ἡ φύσις ἐκ τῶν ἐκτὸς. οὐδὲ δὲ ταῦτα
οἷον παρασκευάζεσθαι πρὸς τὸ πολέμιον ἡ μετὰ ἑτέρων
τῶν γειτόνων σφάλλεσθαι ἡ καὶ αὐτῶν τῆς τῶν γειτόνων
συνθηκῶν σφάλλεσθαι. ὅθεν οὖν παρασκευαζομένους
καθ' ἡμῶν ὑπὸ πολεμίων ἀπαγγέλλεται χρὴ πρότερον ἐν
ἀσφαλῇ τίθεσθαι ὅπως καλά τε πρότερον εἰρημένα
οἷον τὰς πόλεις τὰς χώρας. εἶτα καὶ αὐτοὺς τὰ πρὸς
ἀπόνοιαν στοχάζεσθαι ἐπίσκοπῶντες τὰ δὲ ἀλλαγαλίσα
δε τοὺς ἰδίους τόπους καθ' οὓς μέλλουσι διαβήσεσθαι
εἰς τὸ πάλιν συνθήκας ἡμῖν ἐστιν εἰς ἐνέδραν φανερὸν
πόλεμον καὶ λυσιτελῆ ἡμῖν. ἃ δὲ δώχομεν εἴτε φάγωμεν
οἷον δὲ μεθ' ἑτέρων στρατευομένους τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ἡμῖν
ἀπαγγέλλεται τῷ μεθ' ἡμῶν φέρει λυσιτελὲς καὶ ἡμᾶς τὴν πολεμῶν
ἀχθὲσθαι ὡσαύτως καὶ εἰ καὶ αὐτῶν στρατευομένων ἕτεροι
ἢ δὲ ἐμφύλιος πόλεμος ἢ γειτόνων ἠρεμεῖ ἐκεῖνον
εἰρηνοποιοῦ γάρ τε τὰ πολλὰ πρὸς ἑαυτοῦν οἱ πολεμοῦν
ἐπίσκοπον σὺν ἀλλοφύλων δεῖ δὲ γειτόνων εἶναι, τοὺς
καταβάντας ἐπὶ τούτων ἕκαστον τῶν συνειδότων μυσάγωγία
τὴν οἰκείαν ἀποδιδῷ. ἄμφω δὲ γειτῶν ἀλλήλων ἀσφαλῶς
δεῖ πεπραγμένους ὡς δεῖ πᾶσιν αὐτῶν βουλεύειν καὶ ἐὰν
καὶ τίνα τρόπον ἔσω δὲ τόπον μόνη ἡ ἀγορὰ καθ' ἣν πολλοὶ
τῶν ἡμερῶν καὶ τῶν ἀλλοφύλων ἀνέρχονται πρὸς δὲ
τὸ τῆς ἐμπορίας ἐπιβλέποντα. ἐν τούτῳ γὰρ καὶ μᾶλλον
λάβειν τοὺς πολεμίους δυνήσονται. ὅθεν γε ἡμέρᾳ
προϊούσης πάλιν ἡ αὐτὰ ἄλλων αὐτὰ σὰ τὰς
πολέμους ἀντιδιδούς καὶ δηλῶν ἡμῖν οἷα καθύμνῳ μου = ἡμῶν
λέγονται οἱ πολέμιοι καὶ ὅπως τὰ ἐκείνων ἐχθί. δεῖ
δὲ παντὸς τοὺς κελεύοντας μὴ ὁμοφυλεῖς εἶναι τῶν ἐναντίων
μηδ' ἄλλο τι παρ' ἡμῶν πεπονθέναι τὴν μεγίστην κακὴν <margin>ἄλλοις φον</margin>
ἐκεῖ τι παρ' ἡμῶν γυναῖκας ἢ παῖδας ἢ γονεῖς ἢ ἀδελφούς
ὧν ὁ πόθος αὐτῶν οὖν ἂν εἰς ἄσι γένειν πᾶσα τόπῳ ἐχθροὺς ἐθέλει
συγχωρηθέναι οὐ δαλλῶς τοῖς ἰδίοις ἐπιβουλεύειν. ἀναγκαῖον
δὲ ταύτην αὐτοὺς εἶναι φρονίμους τὴν φύσιν τὰ ἐδην-σως
πολεμῶν καθ' οὓς λέγονται καλῶς ἡ ἀκενώνας ταύτην <margin>πέμπτη πλάξ</margin>
διαλέξας παρεσκευασμένους αὐτῶν. εἶτα ἐμ-πείρους ᾖ τόπων
καθ' οὓς διαβήσονται. χρὴ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὺς παραγινομένους

ἀπριτερεῖς ἑαυτῶν καθίστασθαι ἀπορρευσθέντα ἐφόδον

Τοὺς αὐτομολοῦντας ὑποδέχεσθαι ἀναγκαῖον εὐεργετεῖν δὲ οὕτως
δεῖ δὲ τοὺς καλοὺς φυλάττεσθαι ᾗ καὶ ληφθῶσι παρ' ἡμῶν θρησκευόμενα
ἀλλὰ γαμοῦ πηγῶν νομιμοῖς συγπλέκεσθαι διὰ δὲ τοὺς γεν-

εἰς τὴν πολεμίαν φεύγειν τοὺς αἰχμαλώτους οὐ μόνον διὰ τὴν ὑποψίαν ἀλλὰ καὶ τῷ μὴ ἀναγνωρισθῆναι. οὐκοῦν ἕνεκα πολλὰ δὲ τῶν πολεμίων τυγχάνοντες τῶν μὲν πονηροτέρων καὶ φρονιμωτέρων τάχιον ἀπαλλάττεσθαι τοὺς δὲ ἀγαθοὺς καὶ ἀκριβεῖς καὶ τὸν τρόπον ἀκαλῶς γνωρίζειν τε καὶ πρὸς αὐτοὺς μεταλνεῖν.

Περὶ πρέσβεων
Ἐν πρέσβεσι ἡ παρ’ ἡμῶν ἡ πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἀποστέλλονται. καὶ πρὸς ἡμᾶς ἀποστέλλονται χρὴ φιλοτίμως τε καὶ δεξιῶς τούτους ὑποδέχεσθαι. καὶ γὰρ τιμῶσι αὐτοὺς τοὺς δὲ ἐπιμελῶς ὑπὸ αὐτοῦ δὲ ἀσφαλῶς ἔχειν εἰς σιωπὴν διδάσκειν ἐπερωτώμενοι αὐτὸν κἂν γε τῶν λίαν ἀπρεπῶν πρέσβεων ὦσιν ὠφελεῖσθαι ἐκείνων τε καὶ ἡμῶν εἶναι ἵνα τῶν ἐθνῶν ἐμφανίζῃ αὐτοῖς τὴν ἡμετέραν σπουδὴν ἀσφαλῶς ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ οἱ πλησιόχωροι ἡμῶν καθιστάμενοι. ἔνθεν δὲ πρὸς τὴν ἡμετέραν ἔχουσι δύναμιν. εἰ δὲ μάλα πολὺ ἡμῶν διεστηκόσιν ὧδε πλῆθος στρατὸς εἴη ἀνδρεῖος. χρὴ γῆλε πᾶντον ὑπ’ ἐς γυναῖκαν καλλῇ ἐμφανίζειν αὐτοῖς πλῆθος δὲ ἀνδρῶν καὶ ὅπλων εὐσχημίαν καὶ τύχην ὑψηλά. οἱ δὲ παρ’ ἡμῶν πρέσβεις ἀποστέλλονται χρὴ τούτους πρῶτον μὲν ἐπ’ εὐσεβείᾳ γνωρίζεσθαι καὶ μὴ ἐπ’ ἐκκλησίᾳ κατηγορηθέντες ποτὲ δημοσίᾳ κατακρίνωνται. εἶναι φρονίμους τὴν φύσιν, εὐνοοῦντα κοινὰ ὧδε καὶ πρὸς ἀρνοῦντες ὅθεν σωτηρίων κάθ’ ἕρ ἡ γουλίο. καὶ τὴν ἀποστολὴν προθύμους ἀλλὰ βεβαιώσεως καθάπερ οἱ ἀγωνίαις ἰατροί. ὁ μὲν παρὰ παρχηδονίοις δεβυοῦται καὶ πρὸς ρωμαίους περὶ εἰρήνης πρέσβευον ἀπεσταλμένος ὁμοῦσιν ἐπανελθεῖν προϋπέθετο. τῶν ρωμαίων τὴν εἰρήνην οὐκ ἀπεδέξαντο. ὁ δὲ πρὸς ρωμαίους ἀφίκετο ἀπαγορεύειν τὸν ρωμαίων ῥήτορα ἀσύμφορον αὐτῶν οὐδὲν πειθὼ δ’ αὐτοὺς ἐπανελθεῖν πρὸς παρχηδονίους τὸν ὁρῶν φιλόμενος. ὅτε μὲν ἐς βαβυλῶνα τῆς αἰγύπτου τὸν πέρσην ἀνηγέας τὰ αἰγυπτίων διέλουσιν χρὴ δὲ τοὺς πρέσβεῖς παραχωρεῖν, πρὸς οὓς ἀποστέλλονται φαίνονται ἐπιχαρῆσε. μεγάλο φύγωσι ἄμφω δὲ οἱ οἰκεῖα τάδε τῶν πολεμίων ἐκείνῳ ποιοῦντες ἀλλαγῇ.

...and the bright [part] inside the four-sided leather screen <note>original: "δέρρις"</note>. It should be arranged and wrapped in the center, and of the sides, the three should be of black leather, but where the light shines through, it is clear to those walking well. It is also good for them to wear a small shield, covering the whole of the body while dressed and divided, [for] those hunting <note>original: "σευποκυνηγῶν"</note> and the soles of the feet. One must wear leather [shoes] on the soles because of the caltrops <note>original: "τριβόλους"</note> and the brambles. When this is perceived by them—this, on one hand, for the eagerness of those in front, and this, on the other, for fear so that they do not become lazy while fleeing. In addition to these, one must bring that soldiers be chosen for the preparation of the camp, likewise, as many as are carrying while walking and having struck down an enemy, so that it seems to the enemies that a large multitude is coming upon them; and those who use the capture of the opponents should recognize some among them, and calling out to themselves while pretending to be fleeing, so that the opponents follow the commanders and obey them because of the camp being clearly and foolishly occupied [by them], and these follow. The other part, from where the enemies came upon us, and which leads toward the enemy [side], [one must] destroy, so that the enemies might have a place of flight, or [else] it compels them to stand their own ground, having flowed back from the attack.

<margin>I know this myself, but nevertheless</margin>
Regarding defectors

It is necessary to receive those who are defecting, and to benefit them in this way; but one must guard against the good [ones] in case they are taken by us, and are worshiped, but rather they should be bound by the laws of the fountains <note>original: "πηγῶν νομιμοῖς"</note>; but for the more noble among them, [one should] treat [them] in the enemy [camp] if we wish, provided they have goodwill, and especially those who come together according to the city. One gathers the war thus if these have defected to us; and the less valuable of them [one should] bring with [the] army, where the signals are, and when struck it becomes [clear] as to the signs, as one must trust those many of their own; it is necessary not only to serve us, [but to] send gifts to the enemies, so that in the end [we may] enslave three hundred of them in the march, having sent them gifts, [and] through them, take the city.
Regarding scouts
[The methods] invented for the scouts <note>original: "καταλίκων"</note>, so that by them, while being straightened, [we may see] the affairs of the opponents, it is clear to us to know [how] to choose...

<summary>The page concludes with specific logistical details for night gear, the handling of defectors to infiltrate enemy lines, and the tactical use of scouts for intelligence.</summary>
<keywords>night gear, defectors, psychological warfare, infiltration, scouts, intelligence gathering</keywords>

東國詩教與中州不同中州趨時風氣日流於工細巧靡矣東國猶
尚古法雖有較調不諧用字強然天真爛漫無損其佳也奇庚子歲
與李醇溪念齋昆季會作一書論之今
浮園携示此篇情思超曠所謂神出古異浮奇致者而時露颯爽之姿
足怵人目知其所蘊有不可一世者無感者乎浮園之起異於常倫也魯無君子斯
焉取斯信東國之多賢哉此卷披調不忍釋手誠如所云讀新詩盡青山暮
矣然如浮雲樹色嘉陵心落日江聲襟韻未萬里虞先生舊昔五更霜氣

The red pavilion enters the forest as the white rain rises. The wind comes to the rush pond before the auspicious autumn. When the frost arrives, the tiny evening does not open.

### Waking Early at Cheongho

The water is bright, and I know the energy of the Way is before the mountain. I see the spirit clearly and could paint the new clearing. The color is deep blue as the sun rises in the east.

### Evening View at Cheongho

A new coolness is born after the rain. I wake from sleep and go up before the tower. The fields are moist, and the cicadas sing in the trees. The river is flat, and seagulls pass through the sky.

### Blocked by Rain at the Small Leisure House

The dark forest mist is like water. In the house by the stream, the wine is like spring. This was formerly a place for seeking flowers. Now I am a person blocked by the rain.

De lactuca. Ca. XXII.
Lactuca vt dicit Isidorus ex lactei humoris exuberantia est vocata. vel quia nutricientes mulieres lacte implet. hec in viris veneris motum arcet cuius duplex est species. scilicet domestica et agrestis qua feralia vocamus. quod dorsum eius aculeos habet duros ad modum ferre. vt dicit Isidorus libro. xvii. capitulo ultimo. de qua dicit Plinius in dietis. lactuca agrestis domestice in forma est similis. sed longiores habet frondes. subtiliores. asperiores. et minus virides. propter sue humiditatis paruitatem. et ideo multum est amaritudinis et ponticitatis respectu illius que domestica est. quia maioris est caloris et siccitatis. et ideo multi dicunt quod menstrua puocat et humores crudos expellit. vt dicit Dyascorides. lactuca pro domestica frigida est et humida secundum gradum et in neutra qualitate excedit modum. et ideo eius usus grauisui medicine. subtilibus subam et marie qui erit recens. et ideo cito digeritur et stomachi arsuram et morsuram et colera rubea sedat. sanguinis ebullitionem refrigerat. infomnietate placat. capitis dolorem et fumo colerico sanat. lac in mulieribus multiplicat et semen in viris generat augumentar. et accidit propter bonitatem sanguinis que gignit in pfecta quantitate. et in pfecta etate sed quando antiquatur et indurat minuitur eius humiditas et amaricat. et vsu eius sanguis pessimus generatur. virtus visina inde deficit et debilitatur. cuius causa est sensus animalis mortificatio. quod cum sua ponticitate ipsum suffocat naturale. et ideo talis lactuca generare voletib. maxime est nociua. nam materia gelat. coagulat seminale. et precipue semen eius si in cibo aut in potu sepe assumatur. Duculus ysaac in dietis. Plinius autem libro. xx. capitulo. viii. de lactuca dicit. Est species lactuce sponte nascentis qua caprina vocant. qua ptecta in mare. ptin necant pisces et sunt in vicino. cuius caule et foliis obtusis aspso sale nerui incisi sanant. alia est species lactuce que nascit in aruis cuius folia trita cum polelenta illita vlceribus sanant. et hanc greci ysopon vocant. tertia species est que crescit in siluis. qua steraton vocant. cuius folia trita cum purescentia vulnera sanant. radice et foliis mitigant igne sacru. est et alia species lactuce huis rotunda et breuia qua multi beratia vocant. cuius succus accipitres scalpendo berba ex

Multas alias laudes ei attribuit Plinius in eodem capitulo. sed hec sufficiant.

De lappa. Ca. XXIII.
Lappa est herba habens folia lata et spissa circa terram habens in sumitatibus bastularum quedam capitella spinosa et aculeata sed recurua que vestibus transeuntium solent adherere. Vnde dicit Isidorus libro. xvii. lappa est dicta eo quod habeat caulez in gente terram dispositam et grecis philatropos vocatur. quod vestibus hominum adhereat ob asperitatem sui. et nascit iuxta muros. et ob philatropos. i. amans hominem. quia quadam affectione videat homis adherere vestibus. Lappe species duplex acuta et rotunda ad similitudinem pedis caballi disposita. vt a multis vocat vngula caballina. et vtriusque folia huis et horribilis sunt odoris pariter et saporis. vt dicit Dyascorides. Sed Plinius libro. xxvi. lappe multe sunt species et omnes sunt medicinales. Nam ictibus scorpionum medent. nec feriunt homine si inunctus fuerit succo eius. decoctio eius radicis iuuat dentes et etiam cofirmat si tepida in ore teneat. semen eius inetri cabilia vicia stomachi curat. resicientibus sanguine. pdest dissenteriis subuenit. naz radice eius cum vino fistit aluum. sed sola datur adiuuat calculosos. tota herba trita cum atungia valet et strumae. Duculus Pli. fm Plate. lappa siue lappacii est herba calida et sicca habens virtutem dissoluendi. relaxandi. aperiendi et attenuandi. et ideo valet contra scabiem. pruritum. ferpigine et impetigine. et intercutaneum os sumit humores. apostematum dissoluit duricie et tumore. valet contra frigidas ydropisim et splenis opilatoem. succus eius cum ruthe admistus cerebru purgat et reumatica sufluitate si in modica quantitate

Est at liliu maturatiua. vn valet a postemata si cu arungia pterat. Item ci inest et remollitiua. vn valet a sple nis duricia si ei succo oleo veteri admirtor bn incorpato splenis regio inungat. Item ei est aptiua et copacto z dissolu tiua. et educit purgatoz mestruale. Item inest ei tumoris repessiua. et io valet a postemata et vretositate inflatiua. si radix et trita cu oleo apponat. # Book XVII

<note>A decorative initial L begins the section.</note> The collector gathers the barks of the lentisk or mastic tree at the end of spring, cuts them, and cleanses the area and places clean cloths underneath so that nothing falls onto the ground. Therefore, that which is clear and clean and white is to be selected; that which admits foreign matter and is dark is to be thrown away. It cleanses and purifies the brain and makes one expectorate mucus. It assists the digestive power and attenuates viscosity. Liquefied on a warm tile, it marvelously solidifies all broken gems, etc. Pliny also says, as does Dioscorides, that the lentisk is a thorny tree with a deep root, divided into many parts, having fruit like the myrtle, but smaller and red. When it is mature, its rough wool inside the skin and its juice heal the flux of women.

<note>A decorative initial D begins the section.</note> On the Lily, Ch. XXI
The lily is a herb of milky flower, whose whiteness shines among the foliage, though a gold color glows within. Regarding the lily, Dioscorides and Platearius say: The lily is hot and moist. And one is wild, another domestic, and one bears a purple flower, and another a white one, which is efficacious, and another a saffron or purple one. Moreover, the lily is a maturative; therefore, it avails against abscesses if it is crushed with lard. Also, it possesses a softening quality; therefore, it avails against the hardness of the spleen if its juice is mixed with old oil and well-incorporated, and the region of the spleen is anointed with it. Also, it possesses a cleansing force; therefore, it avails for beautifying the face if its powder is mixed with rose water and the face is washed with it. Also, it is mitigative; therefore, its leaves, boiled and applied, avail for places that have been burned. The root does the same if crushed with oil and applied. Also, it is extractive and resolutive, and it induces the menstrual purge. Also, it possesses a repressive quality against tumors; therefore, it avails against abscesses and inflammatory redness if the root is crushed with oil and applied. <note>Thus</note> Dioscorides. Regarding the lily, Pliny says: "The roots of the lily are ennobled in many ways by their flower. For, carried with wine, it heals the bite of a serpent and avails against foulness and poison. Boiled in wine and mixed with oil, it dissolves corns and nodes of the feet. It restores hair to burned places. Boiled in wine with honey added, it aids the veins or nerves of fish <note>likely an error for "nerves/tendons of the body"</note>. Boiled leaves in wine heal wounds. The seed applied with sulfur is good for the sacred fire. The flower and leaves assist the needs of ulcers." <note>Thus</note> Pliny, Book XX, Ch. XII. Also in the same book, Ch. V: "The lily rose is the first in nobility, and from the kinship of the flower, a noble ointment or oil is made, which is called oil of lilies. Thus also from roses, rose oil is accustomed to be made." From the root proceeds a stalk sometimes three cubits long; then from its summit the flower hangs down, repairing and dilating itself from a narrow point into breadth in the manner of a little bell, inverted in the circuit of the lips, having within as if a thin thread containing in itself the seed, yellow in the middle. Wherefore the lily lacks nothing of glory, as it is abundant in the effectiveness of the fragrance of color and odor. Its color is threefold: white, red, and purple. <note>Thus</note> Pliny, Book XX, Ch. V. But the lily has a root with many bulbs assisting it, like garlic, as Aristotle says in the book *On Vegetables*. And in each bulb is the seed-germ, and therefore in every place it grows where it is planted. Regarding this, look there and in the same place regarding garlic in the letter A. Aristotle says furthermore to the aforementioned: "The stalk of the lily is knotty and curves into the ground, and it is multiplied and propagated by seed and root, and if you do not find the bulb immediately within a few days, you will find it, and from every node of its stalk it emits a little bulb as if that were of its tunics or of the bulbs, namely bulbs of the root, and this is very marvelous." Also in the same place it follows: "The flowers of the lily are first green, then they become white. And if the stalk is cut off entirely from the root, because all the humor of the stalk is included, the natural heat in the marrow turns itself to the upper part of the stalk and digests the matter of the flower itself, and then the little flower expands and becomes white, the humor having first been digested." And therefore, as poets have compared the lily to the human intellect, it solicits at the end for the eternal. Also in the same place, it is said that the lily has no seed-reason in the seed and root, and it differs and goes further, like garlic, and has a seed-reason in many places. Regarding this, look there and regarding garlic and onions in the letter A and L. The lily, moreover, with the stalk newly cut with the flower, if inserted into clay soil, keeps its flower in freshness for a long time. The lily flower, when it is whole and intact, remains long and smells sweetly. Broken by the hands and rubbed, it stinks much. The flower itself, with the seed, holds it in place of fruit. The whole power which the lily has in the stalk and root, it shows in the head, namely in the flower and in the seed. And the more the flower rises high on the stalk, the more humbly the head inclines. Its flower is, moreover, exterior and flat, sweet to the touch, and round in form, delightful and joyful to the sight. Internally, it is sprinkled with golden grains in its cavity, which tincture like saffron. And seven little stalks sustain these tincture grains. Wherefore, it is composed of very white leaves simultaneously touching each other, and from seven grains, it places its seed in the place of fruit with marvelous beauty, and by the benefit of the flower, it is protected by the tenderness of the seed from the harm of cold air.

Why is it necessary to have it from without and from within? It is because the upper union is constant for the Crown <term>Atarah</term> <gloss>the Sefirah of Malchut</gloss> which is influenced by the Holy of Holies at every time they need it. The secret of the Crown is that <term>Tiferet</term> and <term>Malchut</term>, the two ends, enter into the rooms of the actual Kingship. The Kings will spread out into Understanding <term>Binah</term> and there will be different fruits from the servant Jacob and Rachel so that they may take the crown in number. 

The numerical value of Kingship <term>Malchut</term> itself is 40 and 70. Know that the "Small Face" <term>Zeir Anpin</term> <gloss>the six Sefirot from Chesed to Yesod</gloss> is known as "two crowns." One is from without, which is before the <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Loving-kindness</gloss> of the mother, and one is from the hidden Understanding <term>Binah</term>. It was entirely for itself, and the Blessed One gave a portion of His glory to the female forever. These crowns are the two aspects written. 

Do not let it enter your mind that there is any death in the place of judgments. The "Small Face" is the master of the aspects and the worker of the sweetening. For he prepares the daughters as heirs and arranges the waters in the heart of the heart to provide for the daughter, to include her in mercies. In the secret of the worker of the "tithe of the wise," he removes the accusations from her. 

Know that there is no pair of <term>Tiferet</term> and <term>Malchut</term> except when they are aroused. There are eighty branches. <term>Chesed</term> is the branch for the future, like the aspect of reaching the prayer shawl. This occurs day by day. And so in the nature of everything, it is covered in the morning. This happens four times, specifically in the portion of <term>Bereshit</term> <gloss>Genesis</gloss>, according to the reason of the creation of man. Outside of this, they are "two countenances" back-to-back, and at the time it is written that "the Lord did not save," it means the "Small Face" included right and left over the earth. 

He reigned in his place and they dreamed of passing through it. He passed through them to preserve the bodies. Man should not cling to it except in the aspect of "face to face." Therefore, there is no foundation <term>Yesod</term> below in this world, nor above in <term>Tiferet</term> and <term>Malchut</term>. They do not need to ascend to be in the palace of Understanding <term>Binah</term>. 

The branches from <term>Tiferet</term> and <term>Malchut</term> are the six edges. You already know that the letters themselves do not have the sanctity of the Name on their own, except through the matter of <term>Tiferet</term> and <term>Malchut</term>. They have the power to unite in a holy union to prepare the souls for them. Whatever they do not have is from above. When they work to unite in the upper palace, it is the mystery of the letters <term>Yod-He-Vav-He</term>. Those who sanctify themselves understand that the Name is also in the sanctity of the Name. 

However, in the power of <term>Tiferet</term> and <term>Malchut</term> they are established above face to face. Since they were not in their place, the essence of the building was in the wall, as it was said when it is called "the one who supports." He also had help and assistance, which is the letter <term>Samekh</term>, until the mixing of everything. This hints at the male who supports. In the intention of the lower garments, the source of the abundance was opened for them from <term>Tiferet</term> through their souls. It returns to the back from the garment to its source. This is the way of the Kingship, according to the spiritual secret that increases. It stands opposite the husband, for she receives more. They are prepared in their place in the presence of your Master and they do not bless unless they are sanctified by the Name. Thus, a man and his wife among the lower ones are a hint to the letters <term>Vav</term> and <term>He</term>. Their blessing is through their labor, and their intention is toward <term>Tiferet</term> and the community of Israel.

<term>Khorasan</term> and reformed it until it was stable. <term>Raja' ibn Abi al-Dahhak</term>, who was the husband of <term>al-Fadl ibn Sahl</term>'s sister, governed all of <term>Khorasan</term>. <term>al-Ma'mun</term> arrived in <term>Baghdad</term> in the middle of <term>Safar</term> in the year two hundred and four. <term>Khorasan</term> had completely deteriorated under <term>Raja' ibn Abi al-Dahhak</term>, so <term>al-Ma'mun</term> appointed <term>Ghassan ibn Abbad</term> over <term>Khorasan</term>. He reformed it and it became stable under his hand. <term>al-Ma'mun</term> supported him, and he stayed for the remainder of the year two hundred and four and several months of the year two hundred and five. Then <term>Tahir ibn al-Husayn ibn Mus'ab al-Bushanji</term> maneuvered until <term>al-Ma'mun</term> appointed him over <term>Khorasan</term> and granted him a covenant for it. He set out for it in the year two hundred and five. He received news of <term>al-Ma'mun</term>'s ill-will toward him, so he showed signs of rebellion without openly declaring it. When <term>al-Ma'mun</term> heard of this, it is said that he was dealt with through a poisoned drink. <term>Tahir</term> died in the year two hundred and seven. <term>al-Ma'mun</term> appointed in his place his son, <term>Talhah ibn Tahir ibn al-Husayn</term>, who remained the emir of <term>Khorasan</term> for seven years with stable authority. Then <term>Talhah ibn Tahir</term> died in the year two hundred and fifteen. <term>al-Ma'mun</term> had previously appointed <term>Abd Allah ibn Tahir</term> over the provinces of <term>al-Jabal</term> and <term>Azerbaijan</term>. He set out but remained ill in <term>Dinavar</term>. <term>al-Ma'mun</term> then appointed him over <term>Khorasan</term> in place of his brother <term>Talhah ibn Tahir</term>, sending him his covenant and commission with <term>Ishaq ibn Ibrahim</term> and <term>Yahya ibn Aktham</term>, the Chief Judge. <term>Abd Allah ibn Tahir</term> departed for <term>Khorasan</term> and settled in <term>Nishapur</term>. No governor of <term>Khorasan</term> before him had settled there; he made it his home. <term>Abd Allah ibn Tahir</term> remained over <term>Khorasan</term> and its dependencies with stable authority and strong power, and all the lands were stable for fourteen years. He died in <term>Nishapur</term> in the year two hundred and thirty at the age of forty-eight. <term>al-Wathiq</term> then appointed his son <term>Tahir ibn Abd Allah ibn Tahir</term> over <term>Khorasan</term>. He remained in <term>Khorasan</term> throughout the caliphates of <term>al-Wathiq</term>, <term>al-Mutawakkil</term>, <term>al-Muntasir</term>, and part of the caliphate of <term>al-Musta'in</term>. He ruled for eighteen years with stable affairs. He died in <term>Nishapur</term> in <term>Rajab</term> of the year two hundred and forty-eight at the age of forty-four. <term>al-Musta'in</term> then appointed his son <term>Muhammad ibn Tahir ibn Tahir</term> over <term>Khorasan</term>.

...deemed worthy of messengers, as in no way shameful, which he has placed toward the truest **love of God** as an assimilation; but let us love to be at rest and to adorn ourselves through the **civic virtues** <note>original: "politikon areton." These are the practical social and moral virtues like justice and temperance used in daily life.</note> of which we are capable.

<margin>On the Topic of Virtues</margin>
For him, essence is solely "being," because of the absence of all form and the essence of that which is; but perfection through that which is formed comes from God. For as you are of the First Being, so you are not of the first good of the same. For rather, essences and virtue are from this; but only essence according to the **progression** <note>original: "proodon." In Neoplatonism, this is the process of the One overflowing or "proceeding" into the lower levels of reality.</note> from it, which is present to all from God. But perfection is according to the **return** <note>original: "epistrophen." This is the soul's movement back toward its divine source after its descent into the material world.</note> to it. Nor does he demand to be perfected, for he alone is, unless he is a beginning toward the earthly. Therefore, just like one painting from a model, or otherwise taking the prescribed **archetype** <note>original: "archetypian," a primary pattern or blueprint in the divine mind.</note> for the imitation, if he did not keep it with him to record it, so too he who would sketch and color virtue within himself could not otherwise be assimilated to God through the divine, unless he had used that alone to record it. And because of this, my own self will be accurately fashioned after the prototype through the contemplation of the Reason and the model.

### On Virtues

One who possesses the **theoretical virtues** <note>original: "theoretikas aretas." These are virtues of pure contemplation and intellectual vision.</note> is called "God-fathered" <note>original: "theopator." A technical term for the highest level of Neoplatonic virtue where the soul becomes like the source of the divine.</note>. One who has the **purificatory virtues** <note>original: "kathartikas." Virtues that "cleanse" the soul of material attachments.</note> is called "daemonic" <note>original: "daimonios." This does not mean "evil," but refers to a spiritual or "spirit-like" being that bridges the gap between humans and gods.</note>. One who has the **civic virtues** is called "excellent" <note>original: "spoudaios." A term for the person who performs their human duties and social roles with moral excellence.</note>. He who is beloved of God is called "God-fathered," because the soul's state is toward what is called "divine" through theoretical virtue. It is necessary

<column-break/>

therefore, that which is darkened must be assimilated to God, changing from the "excellent" man into the "daemonic." If it becomes divine—which is again "God-fathered"—the one among us who is only "excellent" might at some point also change into vice. But perhaps the divine man is not [subject to change], namely the theoretical man. He who is beloved of God, the "God-fathered," who is seen to be entirely obedient to the divine, might at some point be transferred to the innate, being the very form of virtue from himself, and having become divine in color.

<margin>On Intellect</margin>
### On Intellect

Every **Intellect** <note>original: "nous." In this context, it refers to the higher, divine Mind that perceives truth directly and intuitively, rather than through step-by-step logic.</note> holds its essence, its power, and its activity as eternal. For its whole essence is present all at once. It neither increases nor decreases; nor was it not present yesterday. Its essence alone is similar to itself; for it thinks the whole and the all as a complete whole together. It neither sees the past nor knows the future as something yet to be, but knows everything as it is in the "now." It is not moved, nor is it embellished, nor does it reason through syllogisms <note>original: "syllogizomenos." The Intellect does not need to argue from point A to point B; it simply "sees" the truth.</note>—which is like an echo where the soul reaches a conclusion by placing perceptions. Instead, all knowing is found in its very being. For being unmoved, it could not be measured by time, neither in its essence, which is in its **indivisibility** <note>original: "amereian." A state of being that cannot be split into parts.</note>, from which its essence is unmoved. But the intermediate and middle of these is like an eternal power that has been allotted its substance.

<margin>On Number</margin>
### On Number

Numbers are an essence, indivisible. For that which has no parts is not of the same body. That which is unmoved is entirely **indivisible**. Everything that is divided is divided either by magnitude or by quantity. But if it is eternal in every respect and I assume a certain body, it is therefore indivisible. ## Leaf 1 (Top)

As <term>Vidya Lakshmi</term> <gloss>the Goddess of Knowledge and Prosperity</gloss> is seen, so also is <term>Saraswati</term> <gloss>the Goddess of Wisdom and Arts</gloss> seen. She is the giver of all knowledge and the provider of all wealth.
<note>original: "Vidyalakshmi yatha drishta tatha drishta Saraswati | Sarva vidya pradatree cha sarva sampath pradayinee ||"</note>

To the most auspicious of all auspicious things, to the one who brings success to all goals, to the protector, the three-eyed one, the golden goddess, to <term>Narayani</term> <gloss>the feminine aspect of the Supreme Lord</gloss>, I bow to you.
<note>original: "Sarva mangala mangalye Shive sarvartha sadhike | Sharanye tryambake Gauri Narayani namostute ||"</note>

May there be success in all knowledge.

## Leaf 2 (Bottom)

O Goddess who dwells in the lotus, the pure one, worshipped by everyone, the beloved of Vishnu, I bow to you. O Queen of the Universe, be pleased with me.
<note>original: "Padme padmalaye devi suchite sarva pujite | Vishnupriye namastubhyam praseeda jagadeeshwari ||"</note>

To the most auspicious of all auspicious things, to the one who brings success to all goals, to the protector, the three-eyed one, the golden goddess, to <term>Narayani</term>, I bow to you.

May there be success in all knowledge.

<note>Two circular holes used for binding the cord are visible in the center of each palm leaf.</note>

'गायत्र्यै उष्णिगुनुष्टुप् बृहती पङ्क्तिस्त्रिष्टुप् जगत्यै' ॥ १ ॥

"सप्तसु छन्दःसृचः कल्पयित्वा गायत्र्यादि 'गायत्र्यै स्वाहा' इत्येवं यथाछन्दः" (शांक १८,१) इति तत्रैव शान्तিকল্পे मन्त्राणाम् ऊहनप्रकारस्य दर्शितत्वात् 'गायत्र्यै स्वाहा', 'उष्णिहे स्वाहा', 'अनुष्टुभे स्वाहा', 'पङ्क्त्यै स्वाहा', 'त्रिष्टुभे स्वाहा', 'जगत्यै स्वाहा', इत्येवम् अस्मिन् सूक्ते सप्त मन्त्रा भवन्ति । सर्वे मन्त्राः स्पष्टार्थाः ।

**इति तृतीयेऽनुवाके प्रथमं सूक्तम् ।**

<header>Atharva Veda Commentary [Hymn 20, Mantra 4</header>

The gods, who shine in the sky and possess bodies—"the wearing of armor is only for those who have bodies," hence it is said "the gods who have bodies"—they bound that armor onto their own bodies. The root <term>ṇah</term> means to bind. The middle voice is used because the fruit of the action is intended for the doer. They put it on for the sake of protecting their own bodies in the battle against the <term>asuras</term> <gloss>demons</gloss>. And the armor that <term>Indra</term> created for the sake of victory over enemies—the middle voice is used for the root <term>kṛ</term> <gloss>to do/make</gloss> as before. May that armor, worn by the gods and by <term>Indra</term> on their own bodies, protect us, who are ready for battle, from all sides against attacks made by others.

May the heaven and earth be my armor; may the day be my armor; may the sun be my armor. May all the gods make armor for me; may the hostile army never reach me. || 4 ||

May heaven and earth provide armor for me. May the day provide armor. May the sun and all the gods, including <term>Indra</term> and others, make armor for me, for the king or for me who wishes to fight. The root <term>kṛ</term> is used in the Vedic <term>luṅ</term> <gloss>aorist tense</gloss>. "May the hostile army," meaning the enemy force, being counter-intuitive or antagonistic, never reach me, the wearer of this armor. The root <term>āp</term> <gloss>to reach</gloss> is used in the <term>mā-ni</term> <gloss>prohibitive</gloss> mood. The meaning is that the enemy army should only approach the wearer of the armor in the light. Because I am wearing armor favored by the gods, I am able to kill even that enemy army.

Thus ends the eleventh hymn.
Thus ends the second <term>anuvāka</term> of the nineteenth book.

In the third <term>anuvāka</term> there are six hymns. Among them, the first hymn, "The Gayatri, the Ushnih..." is applied in the <term>Mahāśānti</term> <gloss>Great Rite of Pacification</gloss> called "Gayatri," which is prescribed for one who desires <term>brahmavarcas</term> <gloss>radiance of sacred knowledge</gloss>. It is said in the <term>Śāntikalpa</term>: "The group of meters (19.22) in the Gayatri, the collection (19.22:23) in the Agneya."

<summary>The text concludes the armor hymn by invoking heaven, earth, and the gods to protect the warrior, and introduces the ritual application of meters in the Great Rite of Pacification.</summary>

# De termino Hillarii anno regni Regis Edwardi tertii a conquestu decimo nono.

<margin>Quare impedit.</margin>
Une deale porta son breve de quare impedit vers Johan de D. et count que un tiel de qui a une
avoweson de la moite de la eglise de B. de queux il presenta un son clerc Thomas de S. que a son
presentement fuit receu et admis et institut de l'evesque en temps de pees en temps le Roy que ore est et
puis la eglise se voida par la mort de dit Thomas par que il appertient a luy a presenter et Johan
luy disturbe a tort. Johan dit que ne poet de dire la voidance ne le presentement de Thomas mes dit que
devant le presentement de dit Thomas un tiel fuit seisi de la moite de la eglise et de la moite de un
manoir de B. a que l'avoweson est appendant et presenta un son clerc Johan de C. que a son
presentement fuit receu et admis et institut de l'evesque en temps de pees en temps le Roy Edward
besael le Roy que ore est et puis de mesme le manoir et de l'avoweson enfeoffa un tiel de qui la
deale ad son estat et puis Johan de C. morust par que le dit feoffor presenta Thomas de S. que
fuit receu et admis et institut de l'evesque en temps le Roy que ore est et puis Thomas de S.
fuit cree en evesque de Hereford par que la eglise se voida par que le Roy seisi les temporalites de l'evesque
de Hereford et puis la mort l'evesque Johan de D. ad suer hors de la main le Roy et
pria aide de luy et de l'evesque de Hereford et le Roy par ses lettres appertient a luy a presenter
par la voidance de dit Thomas par cause de sa creation en evesque de Hereford par que le Roy
presenta un son clerc Johan de B. que fuit receu et admis et institut de l'evesque en temps le Roy
que ore est et puis Johan de B. morust par que le Roy presenta cestui Johan de D. que fuit
receu et admis et institut de l'evesque en temps le Roy que ore est et issint est il persone enpersonne
et n'entendons pas que le Roy voille a cest breve respondre sanz le Roy.

Johan de D. dit que Thomas de S. fuit cree en evesque de Hereford et de ceo il vouche record

<margin>
Dower.
Un femme porta breve de dower
vers un tiel et il dit que
le baron de la femme ne fuit
unques seisi de tiel estat que
dower la poet aver et de ceo
il se mist en pays.
</margin>

Une femme porta breve de dower vers un tiel et demanda la tierce partie de un mies et de
un carue de terre en B. de la dotation un tiel son baron. Le tenant dit que le baron la femme
ne fuit unques seisi de tiel estat que dower la poet aver et de ceo il se mist en pays et la
femme auxi. Et trove fuit par verdit de pays que le baron la femme fuit seisi de dit mies
et de la terre en son demesne comme de fee et de droit et enfeoffa le tenant et reprist estat a luy
et a sa femme et a les heirs de lour deux corps engendres et puis le baron morust sanz issue
entre eux par que la femme tient la moite de dit mies et de la terre par la forme de la taille
et le tenant l'autre moite par le feoffement le baron et issint le baron ne fuit unques seisi
de tiel estat que dower la poet aver.

I find myself drifting through this world, avoiding its hardships. My deep <term>en</term> <gloss>karmic bond</gloss> is such that even now, when a woman speaks to me, I cannot refuse her. Everything I think about seems to be connected to this. At the entrance of Yasuda, I asked for a memorial service to be performed. I saw something happening at the gate. There were five or six people there. They were being treated with great hospitality. 

<note>A large woodcut depicts a woman bathing in a wooden tub in an outdoor courtyard. She is seen from behind, crouching. A man, likely the protagonist Yonosuke, peeps over a wall to watch her. This scene illustrates Yonosuke's precocious interest in the opposite sex, a central theme of the narrative.</note>

Inside, I saw faces that looked familiar. I sold what I had. It was a small matter. One person was there. In the evening, I was alone. Mostly, it was a hole in the world. I spent the night there. I saw it in a dream. In this world, things are strange. I went to the village. I went through the village. I whispered. That is how it was. I was especially alone. At night, I was there. I went with him. It was a long time. I met him. I did not care. My heart was with the law. I cannot reach it.

象白山下有雷願子者。慎言語。節飲食。無富貴計。偶有納甲之納。居於九月後。多施其財云。
人皆云。雷願視赤子願。凶凶生之。自喪其家。守而得鄉。此也。故時人云。人皆已邪。三基而貪賤。貪而有生。凡人者。少為甚者。多小計者。為之無義。人貧居一士。必遭凶禍。家運逢一。在仕者遭失。每尋左士者。皆荒居一消。左方俗云。有悖道爭財。一狀大抵惟守臣之。其士進如有貪廉。此蓋因各願於倉板也。
<insert>立花</insert>
公二願。願拂經于身。貞凶。此文之本。養生甚難。其地如吐。守臣不勤。保之養性。不耐。筆月之久。不付之。多受于習。學不專。立下先。妙親上。見所或患。雜顛強拍。速軍運逢一。在仕。訪讀在士。訪尋在。居俗作事。進退之非。不以凶。多病云死。
六三。拂願。貞。十年。勿用。矢敗。此文之。養兆甚危。而取凶者。如計之改過。自私室。若自急之。多責。如儒。必之華。同得之。之少。想極不存。故拘盧之悖。我放肆。禍之。後隆方。宗破核。家運逢一。有喪。若即一塞。在士有能。於賠度。一。其去。其俗有荒。居先。一。狀甚則表之。兆之。俗之。

六合拂發，序貞者，不巧涉大川，此文豈類大臣以養民而國戒，占也，好也。
多事現象，為或永視，守之息或得利，一考不吐，生生不息，事若得
人助也，為受用，守運進一，在仕之因，人生切而位之保，不一的，自主事以稽咎，
在之進取，以人引拔而小，施在於俗，仕為有傳，靠物志，不以之乘舟涉險，
占九因顛，厲去利，涉大川，仕之告人，臣仕天下，至切敬予而盡其力也，好也。
位尊位，至多，恆憂惕，上承天，下保民，至切動，冠之福，深遠不吐，之有
壽福，一人推戴，仰望之多，而為之重，一善士，守運達一，在仕之要，祿崇，在
士必之題，羽在於俗，陽之支，顯乎生，不吐。
○大過卦 大過棟撓，亦有收性，亨。
象曰：澤滅木，大過，君子以獨立不懼，遯世無悶，公震宮，四之卦，為二月，納甲是
辛，母辛，辛酉，丁亥，丁未，生於二月，及納甲之切名，為此卦也。

...and you will have the double mercury of the sages <note>a classic term for the Philosopher's Stone or its primary material</note>, which lacks nothing except to be cooked and reduced into projection powder. As for the white liquor that comes out of the oil of gold, it is an animated mercurial spirit that has the aurific principle. It serves to multiply and to ferment the double mercury from before when it is reduced to powder.

Proceed thus: take one ounce of the double mercury reduced to powder, put it into an egg-shaped vessel with half an ounce of the white liquor, seal it, and cook it at a regulated fire until reduced to powder. Take this powder and mix it with half its weight of the white liquor, cook as before, and reiterate this work as much as you judge appropriate. This is called "inceration" <note>the process of softening or making a substance wax-like</note>; it multiplies the powder in quality and quantity, and one can push it almost to infinity.

It must be noted that with this white liquor, one can make very lucrative ores with gold and mercury, and that promptly. One can make them with the aforementioned powder, and it is good to understand in passing that it is from this single trunk and this root that all the particularities and all the transmutatory branches start.

Take the projection powder from before and mix it with ten times its weight of common mercury, cook the whole together in a matrass for 40 days, then add ten times the weight of this common mercury and cook everything as before. Take the cooked mass and divide it into two, melt one part, and you will find good gold that stands every test, and with the other part, join its weight of common mercury and cook for a month, and thus you will be able to draw half every month to melt.

<meta>This page continues the ritual sequence from the previous page. Having concluded the rites for Mercury (Budha), the text now focuses on Jupiter (Bṛhaspati/Guru). The structure includes the meditation (dhyānam) which provides a visual description of the deity for the practitioner, followed by several celebratory verses (stotram), and concluding with the Shadanga-nyāsa, where the power of the mantras is "installed" into the practitioner's heart, head, hair, torso, eyes, and hands to prepare them for the main ceremony.</meta>

...twice, facing all directions. These are to be known as the **Gurus** <note>original: "Guru," another name for Jupiter, meaning "Teacher" or "Heavy with knowledge"</note>; thus they are proclaimed.

### Now, the Meditation

Adorned with gems like those of Indra, the Lord of the World, who is the life of all that lives. The Lord of Speech <note>original: "Vākpati"</note>, whose intellect and beauty are vast, who is Prosperity herself. With a crown that holds the entire universe of beings, he whose lotus feet are seen at the limit of vision. With a pure mind and marvelous intent, for the sake of all auspiciousness, may the Lord of Speech be well-pleased with those of unwavering heart. ॥ 1 ॥

There is none equal in pervasiveness; he is the Priest of the Gods. The knower of all deities, the Teacher—salutations, salutations to him. ॥ 3 ॥

The Teacher of the gods, wearing yellow garments, the Lord of the Sages. I bow to him who lives as the most excellent of the moving stars. ॥ 4 ॥

The Teacher of the gods and the seers, shining like gold, the relative of the three worlds, the peaceful one—I bow to Jupiter. ॥ 5 ॥

The proclaimer of all scriptures, the expander of all actions, the giver of all success, the god who is affectionate toward his circle of devotees. ॥ 6 ॥ <margin>6</margin>

---

The giver of boons, the peaceful one, worshiped by the thirty gods <note>a traditional grouping of the Vedic pantheon</note>, the supreme. For him whose seat is the sacred grass and who is of golden hue, this offering is made. ॥ 7 ॥

Clad in yellow garments, the holy one, endowed with the splendor of the sun.

**Thus ends the Ritual Assignment for the Teacher.**

*Om*, [earth, atmosphere, heavens], salutations to the **thumbs**.
"One [form] of yours is bright, the other is fit for sacrifice..." <note>original: "śukraṃ te anyad yajataṃ te anyad," a verse from Rig Veda 6.58.1 usually associated with the sun or brightness, here used for the ritual installation</note>
"...like the two-fold paths of the sun." To the **middle fingers**, salutations.
"You protect all magic, O self-dependent power." To the **ring fingers**, salutations.
"May your auspicious gift be near to us." To the **ring fingers**, salutations. <note>The text repeats the ring finger assignment, likely a scribal duplication or indicating a specific rhythmic touch</note>
Having uttered the entire mantra, to the **palms and backs of the hands**.

### Now begins the Six-Limbed Ritual Assignment

*Om*, [earth, atmosphere, heavens], salutations to the **heart**.
"One [form] of yours is bright, the other is fit for sacrifice"—*Svāhā* <note>a ritual exclamation used when offering into fire</note> to the **head**.
"The day and night of various forms"—*Vaṣaṭ* <note>a ritual exclamation for empowerment</note> to the **topknot**.
"You protect all magic, O self-dependent power"—*Huṃ* <note>a protective, seed-syllable sound</note> to the **armor** <note>the torso/shoulders</note>.
"May your auspicious gift be near to us"—*Vauṣaṭ* to the **three eyes**.
Having uttered the entire mantra—*Phaṭ* <note>a sharp sound used to dispel obstacles</note> to the **weapon** <note>symbolized by snapping fingers or clapping</note>.

### Now, the Ritual Assignment of the Feet
