<meta>This page continues the transition from Proclus’s mathematical discourse on the World Soul toward the physical application of these principles. Having established that the universe is bound by geometric and harmonic proportions, he now examines how these "powers" manifest in material bodies and the human form, using the analogy of a physician to explain how Nature maintains the "health" or balance of the cosmos.</meta>

# Commentary on Plato’s Timaeus

<page-num>288</page-num>

...common in **power** <note>original: "dynamei" (δυνάμει). In this context, it refers to an inherent faculty or potentiality that allows a body to act or be acted upon.</note>. Bodies also have certain causes; some kinds are manifest to us, while others are the causes themselves. For among these, some are understood to have an intellectual power, while others have different sorts. This is the case with our own bodies: while some things are visible, it is not always clear why all bodies are subject to the forces that compel them. For within the body, the passage of time is seen in the changes of their composite parts. Since a middle-ground mastery exists over all the **elements** <note>original: "stoicheia" (στοιχεία). The fundamental building blocks—fire, air, water, and earth—which Proclus views as being governed by higher spiritual principles.</note>, the underlying essence uses them, though they are clearly part of Nature itself. It performs its work according to this principle. And therefore, it is composed of presences, the phases of which are counted in number. For while some are able to act through numbers, natural things follow after. The whole universe is seen by those who look, but regarding the elements, these things are not the same. We possess the powers of bodies, both those that synthesize and those that are functional; for bodies were given to us, yet the state of their powers is not judged solely by the senses, nor are they all the same, so that all things are even now part of the same bodies. It is composed of power even in its parts.

For you might say that something in the senses is infinite compared to other bodies, as it has become the means for diagnosis, and is the cause of all these same things. Or perhaps this power has been put forward as either a theoretical science or a medicinal one, like the nature of health. For if bodies do not all become a certain thing by nature, it happens through the causes of **physicians** <note>original: "iatron" (ἰατρῶν). Proclus frequently uses the doctor as an analogy for the Demiurge or Nature, both of whom "prescribe" order to chaotic matter.</note>; for they provided the active causes and some power, or perhaps the entire synthesis of the body is brought toward this. Or if they are made through the ways of the **flesh** <note>original: "sarka" (σάρκα).</note>, it is not possible to define them as indivisible. Just as one might wish for all powers to be authoritative, they each arise specifically in their own way. We speak of the advantage and the division of the beginning of bodies; they would surely incline toward where a certain body of the generations is compared. It is necessary to say that they are as wretched and pitiable as we can imagine.

Natural philosophy teaches the truth. And it is simply this: we see some of their powers as desirable, while another power was composed of all the parts that fulfill such a thing. According to the appearance of communion and the **symmetry of bulk** <note>original: "onkou symmetrias" (ὄγκου συμμετρίας). The mathematical balance of physical volume or mass.</note>. And as far as the sensory perceptions are concerned, these things are common to all; to be ignorant of them is to lose them. There is a method for these things to relate the part to the whole of the subject matter. For instance, things known by us would not have this order of theirs through this method, even if the first orders are from the **connatural** <note>original: "symphyton" (συμφύτων). Things that are grown together or share an innate nature.</note> bodies. Such a world is for us a governing principle. Because we have known whether it exists and what its particularity is, and the seasons themselves; but one must not be so bold as to treat them as a desert. Even if a certain opinion from them was mistaken until the end. Since there are certain—

<column-break/>

<page-num>289</page-num>

—on the other hand, acting as an opponent to everything through the **harmonies** <note>original: "harmonion" (ἁρμονιών). Referring to the musical and mathematical ratios that Proclus believes hold the physical universe together.</note>. From this, the cause or the path arose and continued. These are the distinguishing marks of how things come to be; for they were innate to the universals, and exist through the world, both in the parts and the whole. It appeared as though the things within the ruins were moving into the world. The cause is most similar toward the external. And so all things, if one understands that all these things are fitted together, are positioned as the seat of the **Eternal** <note>original: "aidiou" (αϊδίου). The timeless, unchanging realm of the divine.</note> itself. Therefore, all things have been joined together through its own nature and remain undivided, just as the scripture stands. There is also something indivisible, and the **demiurgic reason** <note>original: "demiourgikon logon" (δημιουργικὸν λόγον). The creative blueprint or "word" of the Creator that organizes the cosmos.</note> itself is handed down as that which is without disposition, even within natural things. Such is the nature of the intentions within the creator. I say these things exist through the bond of these elements. And indeed, such things are unsubstantial due to their nature, yet they are synthetic; for this is the nature of the whole world, that it be extended, and the one seat of all things leads out from the messengers.

The nature of the gods is in those things in which both being and the divine exist. Insofar as the sovereignty of the Eternal has begun, the world is also eternal. There is also that which is governed by the lowest things, such as the virtue of the whole, or even the physician that exists within it. For there is a certain utility in it... or a darkness. For health <unclear>...</unclear> indeed, what we call nature exists in us as living beings. And those things which exist through other bodies. It is appropriate that it is thus in power. However, those who look toward the fluid and whatever color it may be, participate in it, and insofar as it is given through heat, a part sleeps there, and the composition of this is far from the peak. These things, then, we reasonably know to be small, because the harmony of this consists either in its lack of passion or its removal. But the other things within us, such as **loves** <note>original: "erotes" (ἔρωτες). Not merely romantic love, but the cosmic force of attraction that draws the soul toward the divine.</note>, are blamed for such things or for the nature of the divine. Most of all, such things are strengthened by this, and by the attraction that might occur through the holy temple. For it is known through sensory things. For those things which seemed then to be distinguished by a lack of passion were composed in the same way. Already the preparation is fulfilled or composed. It possesses a power close to that of the cause. Or why do we speak of God as the divine cause, seen as a concern that proceeds into him? It seems right to name it thus. The description of the whole world is by nature; we name it, as if nature is the leader of the manifest causes. Through the one who created, we seek the things that are known, or we name the distinction of the ancients which is least contradictory. And so the **Eternal One** <note>original: "ho aionios" (ὁ αἰώνιος). The timeless principle of the universe.</note> speaks. Our joy...

<summary>Proclus discusses how the invisible "powers" and "harmonies" of the Demiurge manifest in physical bodies and the elements. He uses the analogy of medical science and health to explain how the natural world is ordered and maintained by a "demiurgic reason."</summary>
<keywords>Demiurge, Harmony, Elements, Nature, Eternal World, Divine Cause, Symmetry, Physical Bodies</keywords>

<header>Topic M</header>
<margin>The Easy-going</margin>
<margin>The ranks of perfection in prophecy consist of revealing Truths. Sainthood is dominant in the emergence of [the Prophet].</margin>
The spirits of the <term>Paraclete</term> <gloss>Faraqlit</gloss>. It is attributed to the <term>Paraclete</term>, spelled with a 'f', then an 'a', then a 'r' with a <term>kasra</term>, then a silent 'q', then a 'l' with a <term>kasra</term>, then a 'y', then a 't', and an 'a'. It is a Hebrew word <note>likely Syriac/Greek in origin</note> meaning "the Divider between Truth and Falsehood." 
It refers to the manifestation of Sainthood <note>original: "wilaya"</note>, which is the inner aspect of Prophecy. As the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, foretold — and the explanation of the name's meaning will follow — when he said: "I am going to my Father and your Father," meaning "my Lord and your Lord." We previously mentioned that the ancients used to call the Principles "Fathers," but not in the sense understood by the Christians. This is indicated by his saying "and your Father." 
"He will send you the <term>Paraclete</term> who will distinguish between you by the Truth." It is said that his intention was our Master, the Seal of Prophets, peace and blessings be upon him. His emergence was upon Prophecy. Therefore, you see the forms of his legal symbols are extremely delicate. The signs of his comprehensive speech and superior symbols of Truth are extremely clear. This is as he indicated by his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "I have come to you with the easy-going, tolerant, white way." 
"Ease" and "tolerance" refer to the delicacy and subtlety. "White" refers to the appearance of Truths from beneath the fine veils. Since his emergence was the most intimate of the ranks of Prophecy in terms of delicacy, subtlety, and the dominance of Sainthood, Prophecy was sealed with his holy emergence. Nothing remained after him except pure Sainthood. 
My father, the Messiah, said: "The <term>Paraclete</term> whom my Father sends in my name will teach you all things." This means the interpretation of every form of the symbols I have brought to you in word and deed. His saying "in my name" means he is called "the Messiah" <note>The Anointed</note> because he anoints with light. 
"He shall judge" — meaning he shall overflow with the shining Light, which is the elixir of knowledge and power, as previously mentioned. This was indicated in the Quran where it is said: "Then surely upon Us is its explanation." The word "then" implies a delay. He means it is known from the saying "Then surely upon Us is its explanation" that the complete revealing of the truths of what was foretold by the symbols of the revealed laws

### LES EXPÉRIENCES MAGIQUES DU GROUPE INDÉPENDANT D'ÉTUDES ÉSOTÉRIQUES.

En 1889, nous avons fondé à Paris le *Groupe indépendant d'études ésotériques*, destiné à contrôler les expériences concernant les forces encore inconnues en action dans l'homme et dans la nature.

Les premiers mois furent consacrés à la propagande et les travaux purent être fructueusement poursuivis dès le début de l'année 1891. A ce moment le groupe était divisé en sections techniques dont l'une s'occupait de Magie pratique. Personnellement nous avions fait quelques expériences suivies de succès, ainsi que notre ami F. Ch. Barlet ; mais ces expériences avaient besoin d'un contrôle que la suite des études pouvait seule fournir. L'année 1891 fut consacrée aux études préliminaires, et au commencement de 1892 plusieurs essais, accompagnés d'entraînement végétarien et concernant la vision des élémentals, furent entrepris et couronnés de succès, principalement en ce qui touche les expériences de M. Delfosse. Au milieu de l'année, des faits rapportés dans les grimoires furent soumis à un contrôle expérimental et M. Michelet, un des commissaires, put même certifier le fait que le diamant pur empêchait le passage de l'action magnétique de l'aimant. Ce fait rapporté par Agrippa et inconnu des physiciens modernes est familier aux marchands de diamants, ainsi qu'il fut constaté. En même temps, une expérience d'évocation consciente fut tentée par M. M. H. et, malgré des oublis et des fautes nombreuses, cette expérience donna des résultats très curieux et très instructifs. Nous en rapporterons les principaux détails d'après les opérateurs eux-mêmes.

Au mois de mars 1892, en période de lune croissante, MM. H. et K., membres d'une commission d'enquête des phénomènes magiques, tentèrent l'expérience suivante qui fut conduite dans le secret le plus absolu :

LA SETE NATVRAL. Dimostramme potersi di sopra essere innata sete et cupidita nell'huomo di sapere. Et perche la cognitione delle chose diuine e/ quella: per laquale siamo beati. ne questa perfectamente possiamo hauere per nostra industria: ne p uia naturale: se non siamo illuminati dallo spirito sancto: Ilche dinoto Christo nel uangelio di Sa cto Ioanni. IIII. Ca. quando domandando bere al la samaritana al pozzo di Iacob: et ella dinegandogliene: allegando: che e giudei non usano co sa maritari. esso soggiunse: se tu sapessi: chi e quello che t'adimanda bere: tu ne dimanderefti a lui: et esso tidarebbe bere d'una aqua d'una fonte: che fagle in uita etherna. Lagio uinetta adunque do po molte parole l'adomando. et Christo lariépie di spirito sancto. Il perche sapientissimamente al presente dimostra el poeta: che la sete naturale. i. la naturale cupidita del sapere: et conoscere non si satia mai: se non con l'acqua. Onde la giouineta Samaritana adomando la gratia. i. la gratia dello spirito sancto. MITRAVAGLIAVA. e/ tras latione dalle biade gia battute: lequali accioche restino purgate et monde si trauagliano. i. si sanno passare di uaglio in uaglio: chosi l'animo nostro uolendo ritrouare el uero si ua purgando di tem po in tempo. ET PVNGEAMI LA FRETTA dimostra: che aun medesimo tempo l'animo era cupido diuestigar la cagione dello scuotere del monte et del canto dell'anime. Et el corpo hauea accellerarsi nel seguitare suo uiaggio. Ma Statio sopraggiungē do dichiara quello. che ne Danthe. i. la sensualita: ne Virgilio. i. l'intellecto humano: benche illumi nato di molta doctrina: per se potea intendere. Ma statio: elquale per essere affueto a tali chose: le dichia ra. Et pone Statio per l'intellecto humano: elquale si estende a comprendere quello: che per uia di ra gione non si puo comprendere. Et per comparatione dimostra secondo che scriue Luca al. xxiii. cap.

Surely Delos <note>The Greek island where Apollo and Diana were born; mythologically, it was a floating island until fixed in place.</note> was not shaken so strongly
before Latona made her nest in it
to give birth to the two eyes of heaven <note>The sun (Apollo) and the moon (Diana).</note>.
Then a cry began from every side,
such that the Master turned toward me
saying: "Do not doubt while I lead you."
"Glory to God in the highest" <note>original: "Gloria in excelsis deo"</note> they all
were saying, from what I understood nearby,
from where the cry could be heard.

Where the sun turned as its homeland: so that it moved no more. And he bound it with Gyaros and Mykonos, neighboring islands. The truth they wish it to be is that this island was often shaken by earthquakes. Wherefore the inhabitants went to the oracle of Apollo to ask for a remedy. And he commanded that certain sacrifices be made: and for the future, the dead should not be buried there. Therefore Apollo made it immobile: and that he bound it to Gyaros and Mykonos signifies that the men of those islands inhabited it. It was called first Asteria: afterwards Delos. Which in Greek signifies "clear" and "manifest": because returning to the surface it became manifest: or rather because Apollo gave manifest answers there. **SUCH THAT THE MASTER** turned toward me. **THEN BEGAN** from all sides a cry: Dante felt the mountain shake: and after such shaking he heard that all the spirits of that place with one voice sang: "Glory to God in the highest" <note>original: "Gloria in excelsis deo"</note>: which song the Church uses when with joy and gladness we return thanks to God. This hymn was sung by the angels at the birth of the Savior.

We remained immobile and in suspense
like the shepherds who first heard that song
until the trembling ceased and it was finished.
Then we resumed our holy path,
watching the shadows that lay upon the ground,
returned already to their accustomed weeping.
No ignorance ever with such great war
made me desirous of knowing,
if my memory does not err in this,
as it seemed to me then, thinking upon it;
nor because of the haste was I daring to ask,
nor could I see anything by myself.
Thus I went on, timid and pensive.

...to understand. **THERE.** i.e., in that place. It is easy for anyone in whom there is at least mediocre talent to notice how much this place requires that many and various things be said in detestation of avarice. Because if we could free human minds from such a pernicious disease, the life of mortals would be too happy: and all domestic and civil dissension would cease, as would every foreign war. Nor would we take up many laborious cares, all useless to us, which strip us of honor and peace, and deprive us of that leisure <note>term: "ocio" - referring here to the classical ideal of productive, contemplative rest.</note> which we could spend on things pertaining to our salvation. But if we collect what has been said in various places of this volume, perhaps the listener will feel partly satisfied.

<column-break/>

...they strove to overcome, i.e., to conquer the road, i.e., to pass it. When Dante felt such trembling in the mountain as usually happens with a thing that is about to fall, which first trembles and then drops. And he uses this comparison: that Delos did not shake so strongly when it was moved by earthquakes, before Latona—mother of Apollo and Diana, i.e., of the sun and the moon—gave birth there to the two eyes of heaven. Because the moon and the sun are like two eyes of heaven. Delos is one of the Cyclades islands, of which there is such a fable: Jove loved Asteria; she fled him, and obtained from the gods to be transformed into a quail. But Jove, wanting her to cross the sea, changed her into stone: whence she fell into the water and went to the bottom, where she stayed for a long time. Afterwards Jove, at the prayers of Latona his sister <note>In classical mythology, Latona (Leto) was a lover of Jupiter, not his sister.</note>, who conceived Phoebus and Diana by him, brought her back to the surface and made her an island, but a mobile one. In this island Latona gave birth to the sun and the moon.

<image-desc>A decorative blue drop-cap 'N' featuring white scrollwork and floral motifs.</image-desc> **We remained immobile:** we stayed without going any further. **AND IN SUSPENSE:** doubtful in mind. **LIKE THE SHEPHERDS** who first heard: thus we were stupefied; as were the shepherds to whom the angels, singing this canticle, announced that Christ was born. Whence they, descending from the mountains, heard him in the manger between the ox and the ass. **UNTIL THE TREMBLING CEASED:** until the shaking of the mountain stopped. **AND THAT finished:** and until that whole song was completed. Then we resumed our way, and the souls returned to their accustomed weeping. **NO IGNORANCE** ever [put] so much war: because naturally every man desires to know; it happens that ignorance of a thing, i.e., not knowing it, makes war on man: because it goads him and fights him to seek to know it. I did not dare ask Virgil, nor by myself could I...

<summary>This page depicts a sudden, terrifying earthquake on the mountain of Purgatory followed by the souls singing the "Gloria," which Dante compares to the shepherds at the Nativity. Landino’s commentary explains the earthquake through the Greek myth of Delos and provides a moral reflection on how greed destroys social peace.</summary>

# De vita

Hic dicit quod logica tradit modum sciendi in acquisitione omnium aliarum scientiarum. quod modus sciendi est proponendus ante actualem acquisitionem scientiarum. quia absurdum est sic querere sciam et modum sciendi. # De vita

Here he says that logic provides the method of knowing for the acquisition of all other sciences. This method of knowing must be proposed before the actual acquisition of the sciences, because it is absurd to seek both the science and the method of knowing at the same time. Therefore, one who wishes to possess science should imitate the precepts of the logical art. Just as a banner is a sign of victory, so one instructed in logic possesses within himself a sign of power in gathering all other sciences possible for humans to have. This logic is of such a nature that it always makes the learned person wish to study; without it, if one wishes to approach other sciences—namely physics and metaphysics—he is like an inexperienced doctor who first visits a sick man wishing to cure him, and only afterwards looks at medical books. Returning, he finds the disease has worsened, and while leaving the sick person in an incurable state, he demands payment, denying him health and offering excuses for the failure to recover health, thus deluding the man. So it is in other sciences: those wishing to progress without logic do not arrive at the perfect health of the intellect, just as the doctor does not arrive at the recovery of health.

<note>The following section is arranged in a schematic, verse-like structure.</note>

<note>Aristotle gave the method of science amicably</note>
The philosopher grants the moderation of logic as a friend,
<note>he fulfilled, began, and continued the science</note>
Which he completed, began, and mediated,
<note>he placed clear things at the beginning of the book of categories</note>
He edited excellent things at the beginning, the categories,
<note>he terminates at ten</note>
Under the number ten, he causes it in a full order,
<note>the substance of the book, being, and other things, quality, relation</note>
There is substance, nature of being, quantity, quality, relation,
action, passion, when, where, habit, position,
Touching the passive, now here, retaining the positive.

Here the author says that logical science is like a governor, not in the manner of a recipient, but as a servant in comparison to all other sciences. Aristotle began it, continued it, and finally completed it by perfecting it; he first very clearly handed down the knowledge of the ten categories, which are substance, quantity, quality, relation, action, passion, time (when), place (where), habit, and position.

<note>book of species, book of accident, difference</note>
Form, genus, falling, property, and difference falling,
<note>any science, in the teaching of Plato</note>
These are the Platonic monsters according to the documents.

<meta>This page continues the technical astrological assessment of the "great conjunction" between Jupiter and Saturn. Having previously established Jupiter's dominance, the author now details the specific astrological dignities of both planets and the character traits they bestow upon people born under their influence.</meta>

# ON MYSTIC CHARACTERS.

obtained in the horoscope <term>Horoscope: here referring specifically to the Ascendant, the degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</term>, and it seems to claim two [dignities] for itself, since it exists in its own term <term>Term: a specific subdivision of a zodiac sign ruled by a particular planet, granting it "essential dignity" or strength</term>: whence without any controversy, Jupiter held dominion over the entire sky at that time. Furthermore, we saw that Saturn was in its own triplicity <term>Triplicity: a group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element; a planet in its own triplicity is considered comfortable and strong</term>, which attributes three dignities to it. Both are also oriental <term>Oriental: rising in the east before the Sun, a position considered robust for superior planets</term>, and free from combustion <term>Combustion: the "burning up" of a planet's power when it is too close to the Sun; being free from this is a sign of strength</term>, which is a good thing for the three superior planets. Both are Direct <term>Direct: moving forward in the zodiac rather than "retrograde" or appearing to move backward</term> and, due to their direction in the epicycle <term>Epicycle: in the pre-Copernican model of the universe, a small circle on which a planet moves, while the center of that circle moves around a larger orbit</term>, they are stronger. Both are found to be increasing in motion because they are direct; both possess a masculine degree; finally, both are diurnal <term>Diurnal: belonging to the day; some planets are considered more beneficial when the Sun is above the horizon</term>. From this it is clear that these planets, joined together, overflow with both essential and accidental dignities. However, Jupiter seems to be exalted in honor and dignity many degrees above Saturn (for the reasons previously alleged). It is evident (I say) that both these planets are fortunate and well-disposed. We find, therefore, according to the opinion of the most learned astrologers, that Saturn, when well-disposed, makes *men venerable in their condition, profound thinkers and students of difficult arts, serious, with a certain austerity, whose works are heavy and full of labor, and makes them silent and solitary.* Jupiter, truly fortunate, produces *just, honest, good, and beneficent, religious, and reverent men, who are gracious, prudent with sweet speech, and lovers of their own.* And from its mastery, it denotes Prophets, Bishops, *and princes of religion,* Judges,

### Lepidium. Caput CV

Lepidiij facies à Dioscoride non repræsentatur. Peregrinū olim fuit lepidiū, nunc multis in locis seritur à Fauonio: dein cum fruticauerit, iuxta terrā preciditur, & uelut porrū sectiuum demetitur, sed rarius. Post Calendas Nouembres secandum nō erit, quoniam frigoribus uiolatum emoritur, præsertim si seuitia hyemis ingrauat, nam impatientissimum est algoris: biennio tamen suam usque ad annos decem prorogat. Exit, ut Plinius tradit, in cubitalem altitudinem, folijs laurinis, sed mollibus. Vsus eius nō sine lacte. Paulus Aegineta uolumine tertio in Ischiadis mētione ait, Lepidium quod apud nos nascitur, fruticosum est, folijs lauri, longè maiorib. æstate sunt efficaciora. Quæ si tempus anni negauerit, cortice radicis uti frondium uice coueniet. Miram ischiadicis & longis ualetudinibus dedit experientiam. ### Pancration. Cap. CII

<margin>P</margin> Pancration, sunt qui & hac scyllam malint appellare, radice bulbi magni, colore rufo, purpurascenteue, gustu amaro, qui os accendat, folijs lilij uerum longioribus. Plinius pancration, aliqui pusillam scyllam uocant, folijs albis in longioribus, crassioribusq;, radice bulbi magni, colore rufo. Sunt qui Gallis propriè loquentibus sciponiam existiment appellari, sed imperitum uulgus hoc nomē iam cepis communicauit. Galenus radicem tum gustu tum uiribus scyllæ similem fecit, ita ut nonnulli, cum eius non datur occasio, pancration in uicem sufficiant. Omnes siquidem scyllę repræsentat effectus, sed longe censetur inualidior. Paulus & specie & uiribus cōparauit scyllæ. Pancration aliqui pusillam scyllam appellare malunt. Aluum soluit succo cum farina erui sumpto, ulcera purgat. Hydropicis splenicisq; cum melle datur. Alij decoquunt eam donec aqua dulcis fiat, eaq; effusa radicē terentes digerunt in pastillos sole siccatos, & postea utitur ad capitis ulcera, & cætera quæ repurgāda sunt: item ad tussim, quantum tribus digitis apprehenderit in uino dantes, & ad lateris dolores. Peripleumonicis in eclegmate præbetur, propter ischiada in uino bibendum, & propter tormina mensesq; ciendos. Et in summa, potest ad quæ scylla. Paratur ministraturq; modo eodem, morbos omnino quos illa pellens, quanquam lenitas huius maior quàm scyllæ. Radicis succus cum erui farina cogitur in pastillos, qui cum aqua mulsa splenicis & hydropicis utiles sunt.

### Capparis. Cap. CIII

<margin>C</margin> Capparis plurimis prouincijs sua sponte noualibus prouenit. Sed quibus locis inopia eius est, si seratur, siccum locū desiderabit. isq; debet ante circumdari fossula, quę repleat lapidibus, areaq; in defossu cauata, ripisq; undiq; circumstructis pariete, ut sit quasi quædam lorica ne possint prærumpere feminis huius frutices qui per agros euagantur, & nisi circumueniente munimento aut circulari scrobe coerceantur, structiliq; fossa cohibeantur, cogunt solum sterilecere. namq; noxium uirus egerunt, & succum eructant nascentibus satis incommodum, nisi frequenter extirpentur. Capparis cultu uel leui uel nullo contenta est: nanq; diligentia marcescere uolunt. Gracili solo herbas sponte persequitur, fabulosis familiarissima: quippe quæ res etiam in desertis agris citra rustici operam conualescit. Seritur utraq; Aequinoctio, floret æstate, sub occasu Vergiliarum inarescit. Frutex firmioris ligni senticosus & humilis, in orbem prorepit, caule breui, ramis in rosæ modum aculeatis, spinis aduncis hamatisq;, folio circinato horriduloq;, baccis oleæ, rotundis, quibus fatiscentibus emicat flos roseus, candidus odoratusq;. qui postquam excussis decidit, glans extuberat oblonga, feminis acinosi plena: radice nigra, multiplici, lignosa. cortex subrufus ac minime friabilis eam uestit. Viret usq; ad Vergiliarum occasum. Aristoteles & Theophrastus capparim negarunt in cultis hospitari, cum tamē, uti iam diximus, feratur in multis locis. Semen, flos, bacca culinis principales, cibiq; uulgati, caule quoque unà plerunque decerpto. Cauebantur olim genera peregrina. Satiui, cuius ferendi ratio nem ac imaginem ueteribus traditā nuper docuimus: syluestris, quæ hiberis existimatur, quam Paulus tradit & lepidiū & agriocardamon appellari. Galenus lepidiū uoluit odore, gustu, uiribus nasturtiū imitari, nec usquā inter simplicia meminit hiberidis. Paulus octauo uolumine, quod simplicibus & compositis dicauit medicamentis, lepidiū hiberidem cognominari testat̃, nec secreto quouis loco hiberidis ullā ueluti diuersæ mentionē fecit, alioqui nō relicturus si propriū genus habuisset. Addit, nasturtio uiribus consimilē, uerū tertio uolumine hiberidē fatet̃ & lepidiū & agriocardamon appellari. Sit itaq; syluestre lepidiū siue cardamatice, folio nasturtij, caule cubitali, interdum minore, flore lacteo, semine tā paruo ut uix aspici possit, exili radice, cui insit odor nasturtij: uel ut apud Dioscoridem legitur, radicibus binis nasturtio similibus. Sed cum non legittimū sibi locum apud Dioscoridem, sed inter arbores spuriū sibi uendicarit, qui tamen solitus sit res in suas classes distribuere, herbas cum arboribus nō commiscere, credimus calci primi uoluminis irrepsisse hoc caput, & impudenter arborū aceruo succreuissē: præsertim cū nec Galenus, nec Aegineta Paulus, qui ab hoc emerito duce nusquam comperianť desciscere, priuatim huic hiberidi caput aliquod dicarint à lepidio discretū. Nec tamen hanc repudiamus, sed expunctā & uelut luxam suæ sedi restituendā monemus, si qua conueniens ei propitiaq; reddi possit. nanq; nuper ante Pliniū Seruilius Damocrates primus medentium eam appellauit hiberidē, quanquam (ut ait) ficto nomine, inuentioni eius assignato carmine. Galenus hanc plurimum commendauit ad coxendicum dolores, sed eādem esse cum lepidio contendit. Senariolum quoq; Damocratis ipsius prætexuit ex eius libro qui Clinicus inscribitur. Sed Archigenes in quadam, quā ad Aristonem dedit, epistola, hiberidem lepidium & agriocardamon, id est syluestre nasturtiū imprimis prodidit uocari. Adiecit, cū flores, radices accuratè cocidantur, tunduntur etenim difficulter, mox cum axungia quantū emplastro satis sit, coxendicibus & articulis quos dolor infestat non minus quaternis horis adalligetur: dein descendatur in balneum, post exiguam corporis humectationē aqua tepidiore proluantur. Constat ergo quæ tam à Dioscoride quàm à Plinio scribūtur, hæc ab Archigenis oraculis esse deprompta: nec tamen ideo suspicione carebit, id quod de hiberide traditur, ex hac Archigenis æditione Dioscoridi coaluisse, cum nec sedem debitam, nec uiribus conuenientē inuenerit, sed in primi libri calce, ubi locus uacabat, insertū esse. ...when taken from vinegar and honey. When placed under the tongue fresh, it keeps hydropics from feeling thirst. It also disperses swollen glands with its leaves in four days when dissolved. It heals dandruff and flowing ulcers when smeared on after being boiled in oil; likewise cracks in the feet. It is boiled in honey for the sake of food, most especially to promote digestion: thus it also purges the internal parts. It is applied to the pain of the loins from honey. Pythagoras records that when hung in the doorway, it drives away the entry of evil medicines. It is boiled in many ways in a pot, which is cast into a kiln or oven, either smeared with bread or clay, or in pieces in pans. Likewise, it is dried raw, then cut and boiled in vinegar: then it is applied to the bites of serpents, and it is roasted and cleaned, and the middle of it is boiled again in water. The use of it so boiled is for dropsy and for moving urine, drunk in three obols with honey and vinegar. It is given to those with spleen ailments and stomach troubles, if they do not feel an ulcer. The scilla elicits in animals a desire for mating, for if a mare does not suffer the stallion, a ground scilla is smeared on her private parts, which thing kindles lust.

### Pancration. Chapter CII

<margin>P</margin> Pancration, there are those who prefer to call this *scilla* as well, with a large bulb root, red or purplish in color, and a bitter taste which inflames the mouth, with leaves like a lily but longer. Pliny calls it *pancration*, some call it "little scilla," with white leaves, longer and thicker, and a large bulb root of a red color. There are those who, with the French speaking properly, think it is called *sciponia*, but the ignorant common people have now communicated this name to onions. Galen made the root similar to the scilla both in taste and in powers, so that some, when the opportunity for it is not given, substitute *pancration* in its place. For it represents all the effects of the scilla, but it is considered to be far weaker. Paulus compared it to the scilla in both appearance and powers. Some prefer to call *pancration* "little scilla." It loosens the bowels when taken in juice with einkorn flour, and it cleanses ulcers. It is given with honey to hydropics and those with spleen ailments. Others boil it until the water becomes sweet, and after pouring that off, they grind the root into pastilles dried in the sun, and afterwards use them for ulcers of the head and other things that need to be cleaned out: likewise for a cough, giving an amount that one can grasp with three fingers in wine, and for pains of the side. It is offered to those with peripneumonia in an electuary; it is to be drunk in wine for sciatica and for colic and to move the menses. And in short, it can do what the scilla can. It is prepared and administered in the same way, [curing] entirely the same diseases that the other drives away, although its mildness is greater than that of the scilla. The juice of the root is worked with einkorn flour into pastilles, which with honey-water are useful for those with spleen and dropsy ailments.

### Capparis. Chapter CIII

<margin>C</margin> The caper grows spontaneously in fallow fields in very many provinces. But in places where there is a scarcity of it, if it is planted, it will desire a dry place. And this should be surrounded beforehand by a small trench, which should be filled with stones, and the area hollowed out in the digging, and the banks built up all around with a wall, so that it may be like a certain breastplate, so that the shrubs of this seed which wander through the fields cannot burst through; and unless they are coerced by a surrounding fortification or a circular ditch, and restrained by a built-up trench, they force the soil to become sterile. For they pour out a harmful poison and belch out a juice that is inconvenient to the crops growing there, unless they are frequently uprooted. The caper is content with cultivation that is either light or non-existent: for they wish to wither from diligence. In lean soil, it pursues herbs spontaneously, most familiar to fabulous places: since this thing thrives even in desert fields without the work of a farmer. Both are sown at the Equinox, flower in summer, and wither at the setting of the Pleiades. The shrub is of firmer wood, thorny and low; it crawls in a circle, with a short stem, branches thorny like a rose, with hooked and barbed spines, and a rounded and rough leaf, with berries like an olive, round, as they burst open, a rose-colored, white, and fragrant flower shines forth. After this has fallen off, having been shaken, a long pod swells, full of granular seeds, with a black, manifold, woody root. A reddish and least friable bark clothes it. It remains green until the setting of the Pleiades. Aristotle and Theophrastus denied that the caper dwells in cultivated lands, although, as we have already said, it is carried in many places. The seed, the flower, and the berry are principal to kitchens, and common foods, with the stem also frequently plucked along with them. Foreign kinds were once avoided. For the Arabian was pestilential, as Pliny says and Galen confirms; the African was an enemy to the gums; the Apulian caused vomiting; the Italian was more innocent.

<header>D'EBN-KHALDOUN. 302</header>
<meta>PROLÉGOMÈNES d'Ebn-Khaldoun.</meta>

# A chapter on how, when the nature of kingship is established through the exclusivity of glory and the attainment of luxury and tranquility, the dynasty approaches senescence.

Its clarification comes from several aspects. The first is that kingship necessitates exclusivity in glory, as we have mentioned. So long as glory is shared among the tribal group and their pursuit of it is unified, their ambitions in overcoming others and defending their territory are equal in their soaring power and strength, and their goal is collective dignity. They find death sweet in the building of their glory, and they prefer destruction over its corruption. But when one of them becomes the sole possessor of this glory, he breaks their staffs <note>a metaphor for curbing their power</note>, restrains their mounts, and appropriates wealth for himself to their exclusion. Consequently, they become lazy in seeking dignity <note>original: "الغزو" (raiding/striving) is suggested in the manuscript alternatives, which aligns with the context of losing their warrior spirit</note>, their resolve weakens, and they resign themselves to humiliation and enslavement. The second generation is then raised upon this, assuming that the support they receive is merely payment from the Sultan for their protection and compliance; nothing else occurs to their minds. It is rare for one to hire himself out for danger. This results in weakness in the state, a reduction in striking power, and the arrival of vulnerability and senescence due to the corruption of the <term>asabiyyah</term> <gloss>social cohesion</gloss> through the departure of courage from its people. The second aspect is that the nature of kingship necessitates luxury, as we have previously stated. Thus, their customs multiply, their expenses exceed their allowances, and their income does not meet their outlays. The poor among them perish, and the one living in luxury exhausts his allowance on his luxuries. Then this increases in their later generations until all allowances fall short of luxury and its customs, and need touches them. Their kings then demand that they restrict their expenditures to raiding and warfare, but they find no excuse for it. Consequently, the kings impose punishments upon them and extract what is in the hands of many of them, either to keep it for themselves or to favor their children and the clients of their state. They weaken because of that, and the ruler of the state weakens by their weakness. Furthermore, when luxury increases in the state and their allowances become insufficient for their needs and expenses, the ruler of the state, who is the Sultan, needs to increase their stipends so as to bridge their gaps and remove their ailments. Yet tax revenue has a known limit that does not increase or decrease. If it increases through newly invented taxes, its amount after the increase is still restricted. When tax revenue is distributed among the stipends, which have increased for each individual due to their luxury and high expenses, the number of the garrison decreases compared to what it was before the increase in stipends. Then luxury grows, and the amounts of stipends increase because of it, so the number of the garrison decreases, then a third and fourth time, until the army returns to the smallest possible numbers. Thus the garrison weakens, the strength of the state falls, and the neighboring states or the tribes and rebels under its control grow bold against it. God then permits the annihilation He has written for His creation. Moreover, luxury is corrupting to character due to the evil and foolishness it engenders in the soul and its customs, as will come in the chapter on civilization. The qualities of goodness that were a sign and proof of kingship depart from them, and they are characterized by the opposite—the qualities of evil. This becomes a sign of decline and extinction, as God has ordained in His creation. The state begins to experience the seeds of rot, its conditions falter, and it is afflicted with chronic diseases of senescence until it is finished off. The third aspect is that the nature of kingship necessitates tranquility, as we have mentioned. When they take tranquility and rest as a habit and custom, it becomes a nature and instinct for them, as is the case with all customs and becoming accustomed to them. Their succeeding generations are raised in the civilization of living and the cradle of luxury and tranquility. The nature of wildness changes, and they forget the customs of <term>badawah</term> <gloss>nomadic/desert life</gloss> through which kingship was achieved—such as intensity of spirit, the habit of predation, riding the desert, and navigating the wilderness. There is no difference between them and the commoners of the city except in culture and appearance. Their protection weakens, their courage departs, their striking power is harvested, and the burden of that returns upon the state in the garments of senescence it wears. They continue to be colored by the customs of luxury, civilization, stillness, tranquility, and soft manners in all their conditions, submerging themselves therein. In doing so, they distance themselves from nomadic life and roughness, shedding them little by little.

<margin>Koers na 't Eyland Cocles.</margin>
Na dese verrigtinge / seylde men na 't Eyland Canon of Cocles, om aldaar de Scheepen te kalefateren / en sig van alle leef-togt te versorgen. Midlerwijl men hier mede besig was / sagen wij een Schip in Zee / koers na de Philippijnse Eylanden nemende; dit jaagde men na / en ingehaalt hebbende / roofden men de Koop-mans waaren daar uyt / en lieten het Schip vaaren.

<margin>Draak beraad sig om na 't Vaderland te vertrekken.</margin>
Als Draak nu sijne verrigting / dus verre gelukt sag / en herdenkende sijne gevaaren en ongemakken des togts / dat hij nu de geweldenaarpen en vermeetelheden / die sijn Koningin / van den Spaansen Koning geleeden had / genoegsaam gewroken had; so beraade hij sig / werwaarts hij sijn koers / wederom na Engeland wenden sou. Maar dewijl hij besorgt was / dat de Spanjaarden hem aller wegen souden soeken t' onderscheppen / en vermits de groote gevaaren / die hij bereyds door den storm / buyten de Straat Magellaan, aan de Zuyd-zijde / had uytgestaan / hem deden afschrikken / so nam hij eyndelijk sijn besluyt / om het na de Molukse Eylanden te wenden / houdende der Portugeesen koers / om het te Cabo de Bonesperance aan te setten. 

<margin>Wend het na de Molukse Eylanden.</margin>
Maar toen men te groote stilte had / wierden wij genoodsaakt / de Spaanse koers / Noordelijker op te stevenen / van waar wij nog ten minsten / 600 mijlen te seylen hadden. Hier over versleeten wij den tijd / van den sestienden April / tot den derden Juny. Den vijfden der selve / quamen wij ten Noorden op 42 Graaden / vonden 't daar so koud / dat het naauwlijks te lijden was / wierden derhalven genoodsaakt Land te soeken. 

<margin>Komen op 42 Graaden, en lijden groote koude.</margin>
Men ontdekte dan een laag Land / maar also 't selve gants met Sneeuw bedekt was / deed men 't niet aan. Wij seylden dan verder tot op 38 Graaden / en vonden een schoone Haven / daar wij ons Ankerden.

another ship along the way / provided with ship's equipment. Having seized this / one found in it 81 pounds of gold / along with a golden crucifix / set with a beautiful emerald / which, along with some of the ship's stores / was taken from it / as much as was needed.

<margin>Conquer a ship with good booty.</margin>
Thus we kept following the ship *Cacafuego* / which was overtaken at Cape Francisco / about 150 miles from Panama. Having seized this / we robbed it of many jewels and precious stones / along with 13 chests full of reals / 80 pounds of gold / and 13 tons of silver.

<margin>Overtake a richly loaded ship at C. Francisco. Great treasure robbed from it.</margin>
Likewise, the captain / named Don Francisco / was compelled to present his two gilded drinking cups / one to Drake / and the other / to his treasurer. When the commander Drake now wanted to leave this ship / the young man of the Spanish captain addressed him thus: Lord Captain / our ship formerly called *Cacafuego* or Fire-spitter / may now well be called *Cacaplata* or Silver-spitter / and yours henceforth be called *Cacafuego*. Which saying was pleasant for Drake and his men to hear.

Further, taking our course west by north / we discovered a ship / whose cargo consisted of linen / silk / and Chinese porcelain; from this we took what we liked. Its captain, being a Spanish nobleman / wore a gold falcon / decorated with a large emerald / on his chest: this he had to leave behind, along with his helmsman.

<margin>Sail to Guatulca.</margin>
Subsequently, we sailed to Guatulca / and found the judge there along with three officials / busy exercising justice / over some Moors <note>Likely referring to African slaves or people of North African descent.</note> / who had intended / to set this place on fire. We took these captive on board / and we forced the judge to write / that the inhabitants should vacate the village / until we had provided ourselves with fresh water.

<margin>In your seed all nations [shall be blessed]: because you obeyed my voice. Genesis 22.</margin>
<margin>Obedience is better than sacrifices. 1 Samuel 15.</margin>
<margin>Embrace discipline, lest the Lord be angry and you perish from the way of the just. Psalm 2.</margin>
<margin>Prudence shall keep you, to deliver you from the evil way. Proverbs 2.</margin>

"All bound by hands and feet,
And at the open door a prisoner;
And I am called by my right name
Obedience, and so reclaimed.
My cords and also my bonds,
These are various commandments
Which bind the own will
So that it can do nothing according to its liking."
### <term>Discipline</term>
"And I," said she with the file,
"Am called Discipline,
Who everywhere here keeps the order
So that one does not bite into evil.
The file which is in my mouth
Is the rebuke of evil;
I polish and scour everything
Where there is rust and filth.
There is nothing that I do not file away,
Entirely down to the root.
And so that I do everything perfectly
And do not fail in anything,
With this shield of Prudence,
Which is very necessary for this,
I am armed, as you see well;
Thus my bearing is more beautiful.
For certainly if I did not have it,
I would not be sufficient
To correct or to file,
Or to remove the rust of another."

<note>A woodcut illustration depicts several figures seated at a long table in a refectory. They are being served by figures that represent the "dead" or ancestors who have provided for the monastery through their legacies.</note>

"What will be/and the condition
Of these tables/and those eating,
And of these dead whom I see serving,
For which I am greatly astonished."

<column-break/>

<margin>You shall be refreshed before the Lord your God. Deuteronomy 12.</margin>

### <term>Abstinence</term>
"Certainly," she said, "I tell you
That I am the Refectorer
Of all here, and the stewardess,
Who gives to drink and to eat
To everyone as there is need
To sustain the human body
And maintain it in health.
I am named Abstinence,
And armed with the <term>gorgerette</term> <gloss>neck-armor</gloss>
Which is called Sobriety,
By which the taste is guarded;
Also the throat from swallowing
Any morsel that could be harmful.
And do not be astonished
By the dead who feed the living
And serve them devotedly;
Know that these are good people
Who passed away long ago,
Who have given so much of their goods
To the living/that they are sustained
Very sufficiently and fed.
He would certainly be too foolish
Who would not know that service
He had from the dead/who would eat
Their own/and would live from their goods."

<margin>Abstinence truly is to abstain from sins. Distinction 5.</margin>
<margin>Nature is content with few and minimal things. Boethius, book 2 of the Consolation of Philosophy.</margin>
<margin>It is a virtue to have abstained from pleasing goods. Ovid.</margin>

<margin>Rebuke is just when: first it is done in oneself, and afterward it is excited in another. Case 3, question 7.</margin>

### The Pilgrim
<note>A decorative initial V is printed here.</note>
"I saw another pass soon
Toward the refectory going,
Who had a neck-armor
Which closed her throat well.
After her soon I went
And therein I looked.
Several dead people all shrouded,
Giving food to those seated,
And they served them very sweetly,
On their knees and devotedly.
And I saw that the Refectorer
Was she who had the neck-piece,
For she visited all the eaters
And filled their needs.
I wished to know what it was;
To this one I went straight away,
The Refectorer I saw,
Whom I had already followed.
'Tell me,' I said, 'what is your name?'"

<header>विंशतिः ४] मानसोल्लासः । १६७</header>

षोडशाङ्गुलविस्तीर्णमुत्सेधे सर्पपाश्रयः ।
आयसं दृढमेतत्तत्तु विधयेत्सामजसन्निभम् ॥ ४४ ॥
दृढन्येतानि बधीयात्तस्तम्भशाखाद्वयान्तरे ।
त्रिवारमितनैव नरवक्षःसमुन्नतौ ॥ ४५ ॥
भित्वा तानि विनिर्गत्य निर्भिद्याग्रेण भूतळम् ।
यथावत्तिष्ठते बाणस्तथाविध्येत्क्रियायुतः ॥ ४६ ॥
अङ्गुष्ठभागपार्श्वे तु तर्जन्या सङ्गते शरे ।
चापमुष्टौ समे पुङ्खे समसन्धानमुच्यते ॥ ४७ ॥
समसन्धे रथे ज्यायामधःसन्धानकं भवेत् ।
तस्मादेवेर्ध्वतः सन्धादूर्ध्वसन्धानमिष्यते ॥ ४८ ॥
ऊर्ध्वदूरस्थिते लक्ष्ये नीचसन्धानसङ्गतिः ।
नीचलक्ष्ये तथा चोर्ध्वं समलक्ष्ये समं भवेत् ॥ ४९ ॥
षोडशाङ्गुलवृत्तं तु स्थूलं लक्ष्यमुदाहृतम् ।
अङ्गुलद्वितयं सूक्ष्मं पञ्चाङ्गुलशिरोरुहम् ॥ ५० ॥
शब्देनानुमितं लक्ष्यं परापरमुदाहृतम् ।
एवं पञ्चविधं लक्ष्यं दर्शयेत्तस्य वेधने ॥ ५१ ॥
तिर्यग्धावस्तथा गच्छन्भ्राम्यंश्चैव तथोत्पतन् ।
आकाशे भूतले तोये तेषां स्थानमुदाहृतम् ॥ ५२ ॥
उत्तमं द्विशतं प्रोक्तं शतं सार्धं तु मध्यमम् ।
विंशं शतं कनिष्ठं स्याद्दूरे धन्वन्तरे क्षितौ ॥ ५३ ॥
धर्षयेदुत्तमं दूरं चतुर्भिः सायकैः शनैः ।
समपत्रैः स्थूलसूक्ष्मैः निःपत्रैश्चैव नागरैः ॥ ५४ ॥
पाते त्वेकं करे त्वेकं गगने पञ्चसायकान् ।
दर्शयेल्लौघवत्वेवं विधयेल्लक्ष्यं महीपतिः ॥ ५५ ॥

एवं सर्वदृढानां हि गजवाजिनृणां क्रमः ।
कथितः सोमभूपेन जामदग्न्यमतानुगः ॥ ३२ ॥

षोडशदङ्गुलां भस्त्रां छागमांसेन पूरयेत् ।
एतन्मांसं दृढं विधेय्र्गजकायप्रमाणकम् ॥ ३३ ॥

गैजरा(जा)श्वखुराघातैः समन्तात्परिशोषित(तम्) ।
दृढमश्वखुरं नाम मध्ये मातङ्गमन(ज)कम् ॥ ३४ ॥

विषाणं सप्तवर्षस्य महिषस्य प्रगृह्य च ।
मूलामवर्जितं मध्ये द्विपकायसमं दृढम् ॥ ३५ ॥

सूत्रं पञ्चाङ्गुलोत्सेधं तिर्यग्भा(या)मकल्पितम् ।
निबिडं चर्मणा बद्धं विधेयत्करिसमं दृढम् ॥ ३६ ॥

कूर्मपृष्ठकपालं तु हस्तविस्तारवर्तुलम् ।
विधेयदस्थि दृढं नाम कुञ्जराङ्गप्रमाणकम् ॥ ३७ ॥

षोडशदङ्गुलं स्थौल्याद्वाल्कजङ्घ(जाङ्गल) पिण्डितम् ।
रज्जुभिर्वेष्टितं विधेयदिभगात्रसमं दृढम् ॥ ३८ ॥

अङ्गुलं दारुसारं तु षोडशाङ्गुलविस्तृतम् ।
इदं दारु दृढं विधेयन्तिदेहसमं नृपः ॥ ३९ ॥

भ्रमत्कुलालचक्रस्थं मृदः पिण्डं नवाङ्गुलम् ।
दृढं प्रवाह(विहि)तं विधेयत्समं नागेन चर्मणा ॥ ४० ॥

कार्पासनिर्मितं पुञ्जमुत्सेधेन षडङ्गुलम् ।
चर्मनद्धं दृढं विधेयत्सिन्धुराङ्गसमं नृपः ॥ ४१ ॥

करीषधान्यपांसूनां पृथक्पर्णं तु कर्कट(श)म् ।
अष्टाङ्गुलं दृढं विधेय्र्दारणाङ्गसमं नृपः ॥ ४२ ॥

द्वाङ्गुलं मांसवर्णां च षोडशाङ्गुलविस्तृताम् ।
शिलां विधेयदृढं सम्यक् स्तम्भेरसमां नृपः ॥ ४३ ॥

चतस्रः सम्पदस्त्वेतां युद्धे शत्रुनिबर्हणे ।
मृगयायां विनोदेन सोपयोगा महीपतेः ॥ ५६ ॥
चित्रं कुतूहलकरं प्रेक्षकाणां मनोहरम् ।
दर्शयेत्तदपि प्रौढ्या विनोदाय महीपतिः ॥ ५७ ॥
स्तम्भस्योपरिविन्यस्तचक्रयन्त्रे सुकीलितम् ।
वायुप्रेरितपत्रैस्तु भ्राम्यमाणं द्रुतं क्षणम् ॥ ५८ ॥
पात्रमध्ये स्थिते तोये वीक्ष्य विध्यन्विलोचने ।
प्रत्यालीढस्थितो राजा राधावेधं प्रदर्शयेत् ॥ ५९ ॥
खर्जूरीसहशाकारं कृत्वा दारुमयं तरुम् ।
नाराचैः शतशो विध्येत्स्थाने कण्टकपत्रयोः ॥ ६० ॥
पत्राणां कण्टकैश्चैव सायकैरेव कल्पयेत् ।
खर्जूरीवेधनं चित्रं प्रेयसीनां प्रदर्शयेत् ॥ ६१ ॥
वृषलं सम्मुखं कृत्वा पत्रं वक्षसि विन्यसेत् ।
तदेव तिर्यग् मोक्षेण बाणपुङ्खेन धारयेत् ॥ ६२ ॥
पत्रच्छेदमिदं चित्रं चित्तभ्रान्तिकरं नृणाम् ।
रसविस्मयमातन्वन्दर्शयेद्यदुत्तमम् ॥ ६३ ॥
एकसन्धानयुक्ताभ्यां बाणाभ्यां लक्ष्ययुग्मकम् ।
विध्यन्दर्शयेच्चित्रं यमार्जुनसंज्ञकम् ॥ ६४ ॥
अत ऊर्ध्वं स्थितं लक्ष्यमेकमोक्षेण बाणयोः ।
विकटाजुनकं चित्रं नृपो विध्यन्विनोदयेत् ॥ ६५ ॥
अर्धचन्द्राकृतीं कृत्वा तर्जन्यङ्गुष्ठतस्ततः ।

### [Book 4]

Thus, the order of all sturdy targets for elephants, horses, and men has been told by King Someshvara, following the tradition of Jamadagni. <note>verse 135</note>

One should fill a sixteen-finger bag with goat meat. This meat should be made firm and equal to the measure of an elephant's body. <note>verse 136</note>

Dried thoroughly from the kicks of elephant and horse hooves, this firm target is called the <term>aśvakhura</term> <gloss>horse-hoof</gloss>, representing the middle of an elephant. <note>verse 137</note>

Taking the horn of a seven-year-old buffalo, fixed at the base, it is firm and equal to the body of an elephant. <note>verse 138</note>

A string five fingers high, arranged sideways, tightly bound with leather, should be made firm and equal to an elephant. <note>verse 139</note>

A tortoise-shell, round and a hand wide, should be made into a firm bone-target, equal to the measure of an elephant's limb. <note>verse 140</note>

Sixteen fingers thick, made of forest-products, wrapped with ropes, it should be made firm like the body of an elephant. <note>verse 141</note>

A wooden target, sixteen fingers wide, should be made firm and equal to the elephant's body, O King. <note>verse 142</note>

A nine-finger clay-ball on a spinning potter's wheel, made firm and bound with elephant hide, should be prepared. <note>verse 143</note>

A cotton cluster, six fingers high, bound with leather, should be made firm like an elephant's body, O King. <note>verse 144</note>

Dried cow-dung, grain, and dust, separately filled in leather, eight fingers high, should be made firm like the body of an elephant. <note>verse 145</note>

A stone, two fingers thick and sixteen fingers wide, the color of meat, should be made firm and equal to a pillar, O King. <note>verse 146</note>

○ The tongue is like a piece of flesh that is capable of movement. It is located inside the mouth, between the upper and lower jaws. It is the tool for regulating speech and perceiving taste. Its shape is blunt and round, narrow at the front and [broad] at the back.

ieux l'on doit faire à deux de ieu ) ou en

## III.

Aussi auant que iouer conuient faire
mettre la corde du ieu en telle hauteur
que l'on puisse voir le pied du mur de

& ne faire despence inutile, d'autant que les moyens en reserve sont tousiours necessaires en la forteresse, pourveu qu'il aye la cognoissance de ce que peult faire un tres-puissant ennemy, & prevoyant à icelles survenances il n'entrera és fautes infinies qui pourroient survenir par faute de prevoyance & negligence de la force de leur ennemy: Et partant cognoissons souvent que les forteresses pour quelque bon site qu'elles ayent, & fortifiees qu'elles soient selon la raison, nonobstant faute d'hommes de bon iugement, ilz se trouvent deceuës & mal deffendues, & partant ils s'esgarent en leur intelligences, pour n'avoir l'esprit prompt à recognoistre ce que la nature du lieu apporte. Parquoy ie dis n'estre moins de consequence l'entretenement d'un homme d'entendement en icelle science que n'a esté la despence des fortifications, d'autant qu'en tels accidens qui peuvent entre-venir, un homme d'intelligence en vaut milles, & milles n'en valent un. Non que ie vueille dire estre de necessité que les hommes que i'entens doyvent estre versez à la representation de ces desseings, ny les forteresses semblables à iceux: Mais bien ie dis que l'homme d'entendement doibt estre muny de la praticque d'iceux, & de l'intelligence des mouvemens, instrumens, & machines de guerre pour estre prompts selon l'occurrance à resister, & se sçavoir secourir de ce que la nature vous offre, & vous réd possesseur, quand vos iugemens seront capables de se pouvoir secourir en la necessité, pour se servir selon les occurrances, par estre plus prompts que ceux qui n'auroient que la commune intelligence, d'autant que la claire intelligence nous ameine & achemine à la promptitude de survenir aux accidens, sans aller esgarement. Comme n'estant appuyé de certain fondement & de la raison qui enfle le courage d'eux & de leurs assistans, quand il y a quelque asseurance que le conducteur és fortifications n'estre ignorant des remedes & prevoyances, tant des deffences des forteresses, que de l'attaque d'icelles, & des machines a icelles exercices convenables: Et me contentant pour le present de vous avoir discouru de l'intelligence de mon advis, comme aussi des traces de mes desseings, lesquels bien considerez retrouverez en iceux les moyens de s'en servir en plusieurs occasions. Parquoy tout homme de iugement ne prendra cruëment mon dire, que la despence seroit excessive en quelques endroicts, mais qu'il se munisse du sens & intelligence d'icelle, & s'en serve où l'occasion se presentera, comme mon intention est telle, & és lieux là où i'auray cest honneur d'estre employé, ie feray de mesme: Et qui conferera avec moy me trouvera en discours de la praticque par laquelle on trouve la resolution que l'on doibt fonder en soy, par la Theorique sur laquelle ie me suis appuyé pour me rédre plus ferme & asseuré contre une infinité d'accidans qui entre-viennent ausdicts exercices de l'homme genereux, auquel ne manquera iamais subiect de s'esprouver & se rendre asseuré de ces conceptions, pour ne se decevoir soy-mesme en ces imaginations, qui causent quelque fois de grāds accidens, & pertes infinies & dommageables: parquoy ne trouverez estrange si en mes escripts recognoissez ce mesme stil, d'autant qu'à esté telle mon exercice. Ce pendant ie prie Dieu que receviez ces advertissemens, d'aussi bon cœur comme ie les vous presente, & en faciez vostre profit, au soullagement de voz places & de vos Bourgeois & Con-Citoyens, & a la conservation des Provinces & Republicques.

D'Autant que noſtre intention à touſiours eſté d'amplifier & eſclarcir la cognoiſſances & perfection de ceſte œuvre, il m'a ſemblé que pour quelque particularitez ſeroit bon & ſuyuant l'ordre precedentes demonſtrees, de repreſenter le profil des courtines de noſtre fortereſſe de conuenable grandeur, enſemble auſſi le profil des caſemates eſquelles traces & deſſeins ſi pourront dicerner, les adiointes & commoditez du ſoldat que i'ay ainſi demonſtré a pluſieurs fois pour euiter à la confuſion: comme il la paroiſtra en ces preſentes traces là où nous ſont repreſentez iceux profils, deſquels ne repeteray long discours à cauſe des precedentes declarez. Mais me contenteray pour quelque particularitez que cy apres i'entens de demonſtrer, parquoy ayant en la memoire l'ordre des precedentes, nous noterons icy ſimplement ces petites cómoditez & adioinctes qui ſont notees par ſes termes V, pour l'eſcalin & marche pied du parapet du terre-plein deſdites courtines pour la commodité du ſoldat, & encore la cime de la muraille D T, & ES, ſera diſpoſee à niueau, commodité de poſer l'arquebuſe, puis denoterons le cordon d'icelle fortereſſe, lequel ſera au niueau de la hauteur du parapet de la contre-eſcarpe, ou peut eſtre encore au deſſus, & ſelon l'eſleuation de la fortereſſe qui ſe fera ſelon la ſituation d'alentour. Et la muraille au deſſus du cordon peut eſtre à plom ou peu de talu, & le talu de la muraille ſera terminé depuis le cordon tirant au fonds du foſſé, & paſſens outre retournant ſur la contre-eſcarpe au terme O, ſera vn eſcalin ſeruant de commodité au parapet de ladite contre-eſcarpe. Et n'eſt icy en ces petites particularitez beſoin de long discours, d'autant que la practique ja deſclaree, nous donne l'adreſſe de la repreſentation d'icelle aux corps eſleuez, cóme encore il ſe peut clairement cognoiſtre auec l'intelligence que ja on a imprimé en la memoire pour conceuoir l'intelligence d'icelle, tant des courtines que des caſemates conduites & adreſſees auec l'ordre de leur meſure, comme il ſe trouuera par leurs proportiós retrouuee & cognues en l'eſchelle preſente de ce preſent deſſein, là où pourrez vous eſclarcir des hauteurs ou profondeurs propoſee par noſtre conception, leſquelles hauteurs vous ſeront plus familieres en iceluy, qu'il ne pourroit eſtre en la repreſentation qu'il vous ſera faite des corps eſleuees, d'autant qu'en ſi petit volume eſt dificile, & caſi impoſſible de pouuoir diſcerner les proportions pour le regard des hauteurs & largeurs que noſtre conception vous à deſclarez & enſeignez par nos precedantes traces & ſuyuantes propoſitions, & en la pourſuitte d'icelle receuerez contentement & amplification de noſtre intelligence, par la reueue du deſſein ſuyuant la ſouuenances & recognoiſſances des particulieres partie des precedantes, de l'augmentation & amplification des preſentes demonſtrations, recogneue par ſes annotations, & ſur l'eſchelle pour le regard des meſures & proportions, toute leſquelles choſe nous dōnerons contentement & adreſſes des pourſuyuantes, leſquelles ie delibere nous repreſenter par noſtre deſſein, l'augmentation de mes conceptions en la pourſuitte de la perfectiō requiſe en l'art des fortifications, la practique deſquelles nous eſt tref-vtile & neceſſaires pour le ſecours & ſoulagement des curieux & amateurs de la conſeruation de la poſterité.

<meta>This page continues Bachot’s argument regarding the necessity of expert human judgment in military engineering. He transitions from the theoretical benefits of his designs to the practical reality that even the best-built fortress will fail without a commander who possesses "intelligence"—a blend of technical foresight and quick-thinking adaptability.</meta>

...and to avoid making useless expenditures, especially since maintaining reserves is always necessary within a fortress. This is provided that the commander has knowledge of what a very powerful enemy is capable of doing; by foreseeing such occurrences, he will not fall into the infinite errors that could arise through a lack of foresight and a negligence of the enemy's strength. Consequently, we often see that fortresses—no matter how good their site may be or how reasonably they are fortified—are found to be deceived and poorly defended due to a lack of men with good judgment. Thus, they go astray in their understanding because they lack the <term>ready wit: a quick and adaptable mind</term> to recognize what the nature of the location requires.

For this reason, I say it is of no less consequence to maintain a man of understanding in this science than the cost of the fortifications themselves. Indeed, in such <term>accidents: unforeseen military events or crises</term> that may occur, one man of intelligence is worth a thousand, and a thousand [without such skill] are not worth one. I do not mean to say it is strictly necessary that the men I speak of must be experts in the drawing of these <term>designs: technical plans or architectural drawings</term>, nor that the fortresses must look exactly like them. Rather, I say that a man of understanding must be equipped with the practical application of these plans, and with the knowledge of the movements, instruments, and machines of war. This ensures they are ready, according to the circumstance, to resist the enemy and know how to make use of what nature offers and provides you. When your judgment is capable of finding help in times of necessity, you can act according to the situation more promptly than those who possess only common understanding. Clear intelligence leads us and guides us toward the readiness to respond to accidents without wandering into error.

When there is some assurance that the leader of the fortifications is not ignorant of remedies and foresight—regarding both the defense of fortresses and the attack of them, as well as the machines suitable for such exercises—it provides a certain foundation and reason that swells the courage of the leaders and those assisting them. Contenting myself for the present with having discussed the reasoning behind my advice, as well as the outlines of my designs, you will find (if you consider them well) the means to use them on many occasions.

Therefore, no man of judgment should take my words crudely, thinking that the expense would be excessive in some places; rather, let him arm himself with the sense and intelligence of the design and use it where the occasion presents itself. Such is my intention, and in the places where I have the honor of being employed, I shall do the same. Whoever confers with me will find me ready to discuss the practice through which one finds the resolution one must establish within oneself. This is based on the <term>Theory: the underlying scientific principles</term> upon which I have relied to make myself more firm and assured against an infinity of accidents that occur in these exercises of a <term>noble man: "homme genereux," referring to someone of high character or a professional soldier</term>. Such a man will never lack the opportunity to test himself and become certain of these concepts, so as not to deceive himself with imaginations that sometimes cause great accidents and infinite, damaging losses. Therefore, do not find it strange if you recognize this same style in my writings, for such has been my practice. Meanwhile, I pray to God that you receive these warnings with as good a heart as I present them to you, and that you make your profit from them, for the relief of your strongholds, your <term>burghers: "bourgeois," the citizens or residents of a fortified town</term> and fellow citizens, and for the preservation of Provinces and <term>Republics: "Republicques," meaning the state or the public commonwealth</term>.

<summary>Bachot emphasizes that technical fortifications are useless without an intelligent commander who understands both theory and practice to handle unforeseen crises. He concludes this section by dedicating his designs to the safety of citizens and the preservation of the state.</summary>
<keywords>military intelligence, foresight, machines of war, military theory, fortress defense, burghers, republics, engineering judgment</keywords>

Taking the male lead <note>original: "ἀρσενικὴν μόλυβδον"; likely referring to orpiment or a specific lead alloy</note>, I wrote upon a flask with pitch. Take some gum <note>original: "κωμυδίου"</note> previously prepared from urine, and the lime water, or rather through a fourth part of the ash of <term>alamkarin</term> <gloss>an alchemical salt or soda</gloss>. Take roasted sea shells and put them in the vessel and solidify the gum with it. Let both the filling and the jar be bright, and plaster everything in this way. Let there be a bath, and let the jar be like a cover for you, and let your jar be entirely like glass. Set the arrangement according to the projection, so that it may become a master-black color. Place it with you upon the bath and solidify it with the heat; let it burn equally and wash it. For in this way you darken it and the black-like appearance will be seen. Hold fast to this life <note>referring to the "quickening" or vital essence of the substance</note> as if it were the graces of God. Putting it into that vessel, and before the ash consumes it, gild the world-order with the aged substance. For the marriage, give a glass-like breast <note>original: "μασθὰ"; likely a rounded vessel or projection</note> and solidify it, having expected these things in this way. As was said before, put the inscribed matter into the earth. Putting the life toward the breast, add sweet water, and rub the whole breast. For this, having been washed around, will also become a form in due time. For its water will appear there; having secured it, shut it up with it. That is to say, tomorrow, just as you also have the male substance. And indeed, so that it does not fall into pits, but makes it pure; and it shall be placed so that it will breathe out. Attend to the middle of its precious vapors. Again, the bright white things do not contradict you. That which comes from the lead can thus become like cabbage <note>possibly referring to a leafy, crystalline structure</note>. Let the work be smoothed by our art through fire. If it is not so, do not distress the place. By mixing the preparations, a strong, consumable mixture will result and the yellowness will be manifested. It has a sulfurous constitution. Just as when you place fire upon fire, and having molded them, whiten them; and having commanded that it come to pass, it is thus in the rushing of the water, with God who prepares it.

---

This mixture is the male substance for it. A mixture of parts of copper and a mixture of copper. Make the <term>marite</term> <gloss>possibly a mineral or marcasite</gloss> more evidenced; for the rose and the waxen circles of the mission are everything!

---

-> The Womb of the Serpent <-

From left to right: a circular symbol with a cross representing Earth or Antimony, a symbol for Venus or Copper, a symbol for Mercury, a complex diagram resembling a multi-legged creature or a furnace with radiating lines, possibly representing a serpent or the tail of a dragon, and a large Greek letter Epsilon with a bar, likely representing a primary Element.</note>

---

Behold the white sketches; a witnessing leaf. All of them shall be whitened, both the things before the ears and the ten thousand things. Instead of ointments, it will appear running up and tormenting it. All these things, through gum and sulfur under the earth in the flame, result in white and yellow inscriptions. Upon the white it is very bitter; but the black is nothing else, and you shall not seek from where it says to hand over the form to the eye, for it shall be manifest to you.
